chunk_findings.detail: `whole(repo, s)` is a check-then-act guard, and the content it validates is not the content that gets committed. It is evaluated for each shard in the list comprehension, but the bytes that end up in the blob are read again later: once by `W.git(repo, "add", "--", *shards)` and again by `W.git(repo, "commit", "-q", "-m", message, "--", *shards)` (and `git commit -- <pathspec>` records the *current working-tree* content of the named paths, not the blob staged a moment earlier). Concrete interleaving: shard `.ddflow/events/<id>.jsonl` currently ends with complete lines, so `whole()` returns True and the shard enters `shards`; between that read and the `git add`/`git commit` spawn, a concurrent writer (an agent appending directly with `>>`, i.e. a writer that holds no lock, which is exactly the case `whole()` exists to cover — if the writer took the lock `_busy(repo)` would already have refused) flushes only a prefix of a large event line into the file; `git add`/`git commit -- <path>` then stage and publish that half line. The result is precisely what the docstring promises to prevent — "a line nobody can read" — now permanently in the log that is described as the source of truth. The window also spans the `_busy(repo)` call, since the guard runs before it, so it is not narrowed by the lock check. The guard should re-verify (or hash/snapshot) the shard at commit time, or hold the log lock across `whole()` → `add` → `commit`, rather than trusting the earlier read.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/eventcommit.py:commit_shards (whole() guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The hook extracts the knob value with `awk '/^log\.pre_push_events/ {print $3}'` and then matches it against `case "$m" in warn|block|off)`. The config dump in this same diff renders string-valued knobs with surrounding quotes — the golden snapshot shows `log.pre_push_events = 'warn'   [default]`, and `log.commit_events_message = 'events: {reason}'` likewise. For a line in that format, `$3` is `'warn'` (with the literal single quotes), so the `case` never matches `warn`, `block` or `off`; `mode` stays at its initialized `warn` and the `block`/`off` branches are dead code. Concretely: a project that sets `[log].pre_push_events = "block"` and pushes with uncommitted `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl` gets only a warning and the push succeeds, contradicting the documented guarantee that `block` makes a push never leave shards out; a project that sets `off` still gets the warning. (The same failure occurs if the emitted line carries the indentation shown in the snapshot, since the `^log\.` anchor then matches nothing and `m` is empty, again leaving `mode=warn`.) This also means the documented "unrecognised value ... falls back to 'block', the strictest" is not what the hook does — any value it cannot parse degrades to `warn`. The extraction needs to strip quotes (e.g. `sed "s/'//g"`/`tr -d "'"`) and tolerate indentation rather than assuming a bare `$3`.
chunk_findings.title: scripts/ci/pre-push:35-36

chunk_findings.detail: The test proves "warn does not block the push" only by asserting the literal token `refused` is absent from stderr. A pre-push hook exits non-zero to abort the push, so the real property is `returncode == 0`; this assertion never checks it. Concretely, an implementation whose warn branch prints `... not committed ... (warning)` and then `sys.exit(1)` (or otherwise returns 1) blocks every push while still containing `"not committed"` in stderr and no `"refused"` token — the test passes although the default mode is blocking. The test should assert `p.returncode == 0` in addition to the message check.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_events_committed_doors.py::test_pre_push_warn_mode_does_not_refuse_for_the_shards

chunk_findings.detail: The test only asserts that the warning text is absent from stderr; it never checks the exit status. An `off` mode that crashes or is misparsed (e.g. the config lookup fails and the hook exits 1 without printing `not committed`) passes this test while silently aborting every push. Asserting `p.returncode == 0` would make the "off means the hook does nothing" contract testable.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_events_committed_doors.py::test_pre_push_off_is_silent

Where it cannot (instruction-text-only agents), the safeguard is delivered as text and the parity report lists it as not enforceable on that harness; nothing is reported as enforced that is not. data.body: Detect imports in the item's globs (Python ast first, JS/TS next) and pinned versions from uv.lock, poetry.lock, requirements, package-lock; a card is the few symbols the item likely uses: signature, one-line usage, 'changed or deprecated since', with provenance (source, retrieved, version) and size caps (knobs); stored in a cache keyed by package, version and symbol set, invalidated on a lock change; sources in order: the installed package's own docstrings and --help, project docs, llms.txt, a companion (context7) when one is reachable. A card says UNAVAILABLE when no source answered, never a guess.
data.title: Version-pinned API cards for the libraries an item touches: detected from imports and lock files, cached, refreshed when a version changes

data.body: Because only the agent can call another MCP server, a safeguard with action consult names the exact call: e.g. context7 resolve-library-id then query-docs for library X topic Y (from the detected imports), or the codeguide resource for language L; only when the companion is registered for that harness (ddflow companions), else it falls back to the cards or proposes the install. Compliance: where the harness has a post_tool rung the call is seen and recorded in the delivery trail (tool, argument digest); elsewhere compliance is UNAVAILABLE and said so. The companion serves the gate AND the authoring moment from then on.
data.title: A consult action: tell the agent which companion call to make before writing (context7 library docs, codeguide standards resource), and record whether it did

data.body: Falsifiable claim: a stdlib stdio MCP client in ddflow can fetch context7 and codeguide content into the card cache cheaper and more reliably than asking each agent to consult. Probe: a minimal client against both servers (launch via npx, initialize, list, call), measured latency, failure modes, offline behaviour, what it costs per refresh. Security: launching a companion is running a command; launch lines only from the operator's local layer or allowlist (never committed config), as for the lane launcher. Verdict decides whether a build task is filed; do not build before the verdict.
data.title: Research: should ddflow be an MCP client itself, to fetch and cache cards from companions deterministically?

data.body: The standards gate gains card-aware evidence: ruff/mypy/eslint findings are tagged with the card that said it; an import that does not resolve or a symbol missing or deprecated in the PINNED version (static check against the installed package) is an API-drift finding; ddflow controls drift ranks cards by violations caught, models and tiers by drift rate. A card never violated costs tokens for nothing and is a candidate to drop; one violated often is strengthened or moved earlier. Feeds P-governor.tier-feedback.

data.text: Ask me the questions

Answers (AskUserQuestion, 2026-10-12): safeguard = a separate safeguard kind; weakening = an agent may weaken its own task's scope (with a reason), everything else operator; card cache = committed; lesson duty = warn by default

data.decision: Operator 2026-10-12 (AskUserQuestion). (1) A safeguard is its own record kind (trigger, audience, action, params, envelope), declared on the shared RecordKind descriptor like every kind: its own CLI group (ddflow safeguard) and ONE MCP tool (ddflow_safeguard, verbs as actions), with list, show, add, edit, remove, history, supersede, merge, split and restore from the record contract; a safeguard may cite the rules, decisions and lessons it came from; rules stay text. (2) WEAKENING: the operator may weaken, disable, remove or widen anything. An AGENT may waive a safeguard only for the ONE item it holds, with a reason: a task-scoped waiver recorded as an event, shown in the brief and by ddflow controls, expiring when the item completes or is released; a safeguard marked non_waivable (for example ask before pushing) cannot be waived by an agent; everything wider needs the operator and is held until acknowledged. This is a deliberate narrow exception to D-decision-management (waivers of decisions and goals stay operator-only). (3) CARDS (style and API) are COMMITTED to the repository (.ddflow/cards/, one file per card keyed by package and version or by config digest, so two branches rarely touch one file), regenerated from lock files and tool configs, declared as regenerated paths (no lease conflicts, regenerate after a merge, never text-merged), with size caps as knobs. (4) LESSON DUTY: closing a bug warns when no lesson is recorded (add one or pass --no-lesson --reason; the reason is logged); lessons.require_lesson_on_bug = off|warn|block, default warn. All values are knobs and every change is logged (D-everything-configurable).
data.title: Safeguards: a separate record kind; an agent may waive one for its own task; cards are committed; a closed bug warns without a lesson

data.body: D-safeguards (operator 2026-10-12): a SAFEGUARD IS ITS OWN RECORD KIND, not an extension of rules. Fields: id, title, text (short, token-capped), trigger (session_start|claim|dispatch|gate:<id>|pre_tool|pre_commit|merge), audience (agent, role, harness, model tier, subagent), action (inject|consult|require_ack|require_approval|refuse|cap), params, envelope (allowed_tools, allowed_skills, write_globs, max_turns, max_tokens, max_spend), non_waivable flag, cites (rule, decision and lesson ids it came from), status. Declared on the RecordKind descriptor (P-record-contract): CLI group ddflow safeguard, ONE MCP tool ddflow_safeguard (verbs as actions, tool-budget aware), list/show/add/edit/remove/history/supersede/merge/split/restore from the contract. A refuse or cap action needs a trigger the harness ladder can enforce, else it is stored with a 'cannot enforce here' note per harness (never treated as active). Rules stay plain text and keep their verbs; ddflow safeguard import-rule turns a rule into a safeguard when the user asks. Knobs: [safeguards] default trigger, max injected size per door, which actions an agent may add (stricter only).
data.title: Define the safeguard record kind: trigger, audience, action, params and envelope, on the shared descriptor with its own CLI group and one MCP tool (D-safeguards)

data.body: ddflow controls [--for session|lane|item|agent] shows, in one table: active safeguards (and where each came from), subagent definitions and their envelopes, skills in force, last delivery, last change (who, when, why, prompt), cost per entry (tokens always loaded, last dispatch spend, tier). controls explain <session> answers 'what governed this session and why'. One engine behind CLI and MCP; edits go through the owning verbs (safeguard, rule, agent, skill), never a second write path; every row links to its history.

A subagent, skill or role definition carries an optional envelope: allowed_tools, allowed_skills, write_globs (default the item's globs, B-sub-sod), max_turns, max_tokens, max_spend (tokens and turns first, as D-gap-defaults). It is WRITTEN into the harness agent file where the harness supports tools/permission fields (descriptor-driven), TOLD in the dispatch brief everywhere, ENFORCED by flags when ddflow launches the agent (P-agent-parity.launcher: --max-turns), and CHECKED after the fact against the usage ledger (B-gap-spend) with a doctor note when exceeded. Widening an envelope is operator-only (B-sub-trust); the only agent relaxation is the one-item waiver of P-safeguards.waiver.

Exact numbers and rules, not paraphrase: 'line length 100, double quotes, import order isort, no print' read from [tool.ruff] and friends, one short card per language and path scope, delivered at claim and dispatch through the safeguard inject path; regenerated when the config digest changes; the standards gate checks the same configs, so the agent sees before writing what the gate enforces after. No network, no companion needed. CACHE (operator 2026-10-12): cards are COMMITTED under .ddflow/cards/, one file per card keyed by package and version (api) or config digest (style), so two branches rarely touch one file; declared as regenerated paths (no lease conflicts; regenerate after a merge, never text-merge: P-change-surface.pins concept); size caps are knobs.

Detect imports in the item's globs (Python ast first, JS/TS next) and pinned versions from uv.lock, poetry.lock, requirements, package-lock; a card is the few symbols the item likely uses: signature, one-line usage, 'changed or deprecated since', with provenance (source, retrieved, version) and size caps (knobs); stored in a cache keyed by package, version and symbol set, invalidated on a lock change; sources in order: the installed package's own docstrings and --help, project docs, llms.txt, a companion (context7) when one is reachable. A card says UNAVAILABLE when no source answered, never a guess. CACHE (operator 2026-10-12): cards are COMMITTED under .ddflow/cards/, one file per card keyed by package and version (api) or config digest (style), so two branches rarely touch one file; declared as regenerated paths (no lease conflicts; regenerate after a merge, never text-merge: P-change-surface.pins concept); size caps are knobs.

ddflow safeguard waive <id> --item <held item> --reason ... (CLI and MCP, same verb): an event safeguard.waived {safeguard, item, agent, reason}, only for an item the caller holds a live lease on, refused for a non_waivable safeguard (exit 3, explained), shown in the brief, by ddflow controls and in the dispatch brief, expires at complete, release or abandon, never carries over to another item or agent. Everything wider (disable, remove, edit, widen an envelope, waive for several items) is held for the operator. A deliberate narrow exception to D-decision-management (waivers of decisions stay operator-only). Regression: a waiver on one item does not weaken the same safeguard on another.

data.body: A shipped /safeguard command and MCP prompt turns a sentence into the exact safeguard fields, shows what it will govern and the harness rungs that can enforce it, and applies it only after a yes through the same ddflow safeguard verb; logged with the prompt (config.changed-style event, D-everything-configurable).

Operator 2026-10-12: research how to manage subagents, skills and safeguards, insert safeguards when tasks or sessions start, let the user delete, edit, modify, review and log everything by CLI and MCP on shared code, and improve cost and complexity management. Research R-safeguards (CONFIRMED). Builds on, never duplicates: P-subagents (registry, sync, route, separation of duties, trust, metrics), P-skills (model, events, authoring, sync, doctor, context), the rules machinery (shipped CRUD, injected by glob), P-record-contract (one lifecycle for every kind), P-governor (tiers, quotas, floors), B-gap-spend (usage ledger) and P-agent-parity (hook rungs per harness). New: the safeguard (trigger, audience, action, envelope) as its OWN record kind on the shared descriptor (D-safeguards), a task-scoped waiver, delivery evidence, dispatch briefs, capability and cost envelopes, one review view, shipped default safeguards. All values are knobs (D-everything-configurable); small modules (D-small-files). DECIDED 2026-10-12: D-safeguards (separate kind; an agent may waive for its own task only; cards committed; bug close warns without a lesson).

chunk_findings.detail: The hook reads the knob with `awk '/^log\.pre_push_events/ {print $3}'` and then matches that against `case "$m" in warn|block|off)`. The config dump this same change ships renders string knobs with surrounding quotes — the README knob table added by this diff literally lists `| log.pre_push_events | "warn" | ... |` and `| log.commit_events_message | "events: {reason}" |`, and the golden snapshot shows `log.pre_push_events = 'warn' [default]`. For such a line `$3` is `'warn'` (quotes included), which matches none of `warn|block|off`; the mode is therefore never set from config, so `block` cannot block a push and the intended `off`/`warn` semantics are lost. Nothing in the visible diff changes the awk expression or the rendering pipeline, so the mismatch stands.

chunk_findings.detail: `whole(repo, s)` is a check-then-act guard, and the bytes it validates are not the bytes committed: the content is re-read by `git add -- *shards` and again by `git commit -- *shards`, and `git commit -- <pathspec>` records the *current working-tree* content of the named paths, not the blob staged moments earlier. A concurrent writer that appends to a shard between the `whole()` check and the `commit` lands a shard whose last line does not parse (the very case `whole()` exists to skip) inside the event commit. The diff does not add a re-validation or a snapshot of the staged content, so the guard remains racy.

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts only that the literal token `refused` is absent from stderr. (warning)` and then `sys.exit(1)` contains `not committed` and no `refused`, so it passes while blocking every push. No change to this assertion appears in the diff.

The snapshot under review prints the knob as an object field (`"key": "log.pre_push_events",` on one line, `"value": "warn",` on the next), so the `^log\.pre_push_events` regex does not match a line at all and `$3` is empty; the flat rendering quoted by the earlier review (`log.pre_push_events = 'warn' [default]`) makes `$3` the literal `'warn'` including the quotes. In both cases no arm of the `case` fires and the push falls to whatever the default arm does, not to the configured mode — so a project that explicitly sets `off` can still get a warning or a refusal, and `block` is not guaranteed to refuse. Nothing in this hunk (a golden snapshot) changes that extraction or matching.

chunk_findings.detail: The test still proves "warn does not block" only by asserting the literal token `refused` is absent from stderr, not by asserting the exit status. A pre-push hook aborts a push by exiting non-zero, so the property under test is `returncode == 0`. An implementation whose warn branch prints `... not committed ... (warning)` and then exits 1 blocks every push while containing neither the word `refused` nor (per the asserted token) anything that fails the assertion, so the test passes while the feature is broken. This hunk does not modify the test file, so the gap remains.

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts only that the warning text is missing from stderr and never checks the exit status. An `off` path that is misparsed (see the HIGH finding above) and exits 1 without printing `not committed` passes this test while silently aborting every push, which is exactly the failure mode `off` is meant to rule out. Asserting `p.returncode == 0` would make the contract testable; the test file is untouched by this hunk, so the finding stands.

chunk_findings.detail: The content validated by `whole(repo, s)` is not the content that gets committed: the guard runs in the list comprehension, but the bytes recorded are read again afterwards by `W.git(repo, "add", "--", *shards)` and again when `git commit -- <pathspec>` writes the *current working-tree* content of the named paths rather than the blob staged a moment earlier. Between the check and the commit any concurrent writer to `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl` changes what the guard approved, so the guard's "this shard is intact" verdict can be false for the object that lands in history. This hunk contains only the regenerated transcript and makes no change to `commit_shards`, so the check-then-act window is unchanged.

chunk_findings.detail: The golden snapshot in this very diff renders string-valued knobs quoted: `log.pre_push_events = 'warn'   [default]`, `log.commit_events_message = 'events: {reason}'   [default]`, `log.pre_push_events` fallback text aside. The hook takes the knob value with `awk '/^log\.pre_push_events/ {print $3}'` and then `case "$m" in warn|block|off)`. For the documented rendering, `$3` is the four-character string `'warn'` *including the literal single quotes*, which matches none of the `case` arms. Concretely: with the default (`log.pre_push_events` unset) the hook extracts `'warn'`, falls through the `case`, prints nothing and exits 0 — the promised "warn (default) names them" never happens, and a project that sets `block` gets a silent no-op push instead of a refusal. Nothing in the author's triage (untriaged) or in this diff changes the renderer or the hook, so the finding stands; the fix cannot be "change the dump", because this snapshot records the dump's contract. The hook must strip quotes (`tr -d "'"` / `sed "s/^'//;s/'$//"`) or read the knob through `ddflow config --get`/the TOML layer rather than by `awk`-field index.

chunk_findings.detail: The event-log commit is issued before the after-merge check: `committed = EC.commit_at(log, cfg, "merge", f"merge {item}")` sits immediately above `ci_after = check_after_merge(repo, sha=sha, item=item, agent=agent)`. `check_after_merge` is handed `item` and `agent`, i.e. it is the step that attributes/records the CI outcome for this merge in the event log, so it appends a shard under `.ddflow/events/`. Because the commit already ran, that shard is not part of the commit: after a normal merge whose after-merge check records its result, the primary checkout still has a dirty/untracked `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl`, so `doctor` still reports uncommitted shards and the pre-push hook still warns about main lacking shards present in the working tree — precisely the failure this change is supposed to fix. The intent says ddflow commits the shards it wrote "at merge/complete/release/stop", i.e. as the last event-producing step of the command; the call needs to move after `check_after_merge` (otherwise only the pre-CI shards are ever committed and every merge leaves new uncommitted shards behind).

An append to a shard between the guard and the commit therefore lands in git without having been validated. `whole(repo, s)` is a check-then-act guard whose validated content is not the content committed: the bytes are read again by `W.git(repo, "add", "--", *shards)` and, decisively, by `W.git(repo, "commit", ..., "--", *shards)` — `git commit -- <pathspec>` records the *current working-tree* content of the named paths, not the blob staged a moment earlier. Concrete interleaving: while the door is committing, the shard writer (another session/process per the per-worktree-identity design this change introduces) appends to `s` between the `whole()` read and the `commit` read, so an unvalidated (possibly torn, last-line-partial) shard is committed to the source of truth. Nothing in the reviewed diff re-reads and re-validates at commit time or commits from the index (`git commit` without a pathspec after `whole()` re-validation), so the finding still holds.

chunk_findings.detail: The lookup `ddflow config --filter log.pre_push_events | awk '/^log\.pre_push_events/ {print $3}'` anchors the match at column 0 (`^log\.`), but the config dump this same diff renders is indented. The golden snapshot added in this diff shows the knob line as `      log.pre_push_events = 'warn'   [default]` (six leading spaces, as all other `key = value   [default]` lines in the same snapshot are indented). If `--filter` output preserves that line formatting, the awk pattern never matches, `m` is empty, `case "$m" in …` falls through, and `mode` keeps its hardcoded `warn` default. Concretely: a project that sets `log.pre_push_events = 'block'` (or `'off'`) still gets only the warning branch — `block_events` stays 0, the `exit 1` is never reached, and the push goes through with the uncommitted shards, while `off` still prints the warning. Every knob value is therefore inert; only the default behaves as if set. The added `tr -d "'\""` fixes the quoting of `$3` but does nothing about the `^` anchor, so it does not answer this. Either drop the anchor (`/log\.pre_push_events/`) or anchor after optional whitespace (`/^[[:space:]]*log\.pre_push_events/`), and the golden line format should be used as the reference.

A live writer that appends a partial line to `live-writer.jsonl` between the `whole()` check and the commit causes that half-written tail to be committed, which is exactly what the "skip half-written shards" contract forbids. The new `test_a_half_written_shard_is_skipped_not_committed` only exercises a statically half-written file, so it does not probe the check-then-act window and does not answer this finding.

The hook extracts the value with `awk '/^log\.pre_push_events/ {print $3}'`, i.e. field 3 of that line, which is `'warn'` including the literal quotes, then matches it with `case "$m" in warn|block|off)`. data.text: Yes, install it

data.claim: opencode runs subagents SYNCHRONOUSLY by default, which blocks the parent session (the behaviour the operator saw on Kilo, the same engine family), and its own server API offers the escape: a child-session tree, an experimental route that detaches blocking subagents into the background, abort, interrupt, wait, prompt_async and parallel sessions under one server
data.falsifier: the background route or the children route is absent in 1.19.0, or two sessions cannot exist at once under one server
data.mechanism: opencode serve exposes two API surfaces: the legacy /session routes and a newer /api/session routes; subagents are child sessions of the parent (GET /session/{id}/children); POST /experimental/session/{id}/background is documented as 'Detach any synchronous subagents currently blocking the session and continue them in the background'
data.probe: npm install [REDACTED:email] into a scratch directory with an isolated HOME and XDG dirs; opencode --help; opencode serve --port 47811 --pure; curl /session, POST /session twice, POST /session/{id}/abort, GET /doc and read the operation descriptions; the same on the installed Kilo 7.2.20
data.probe_output: opencode 1.19.0 installed and running; commands include acp (Agent Client Protocol server), serve, attach <url>, run, session, export/import, plugin, db, --pure (no external plugins); two parallel sessions created under one server; abort on an idle session returned true [200]; /doc lists 162 paths: legacy GET,POST /session, GET /session/status, GET /session/{id}/children, POST /session/{id}/prompt_async ('returning immediately'), POST /session/{id}/abort, /fork, /summarize, /command, /shell, /diff, /permissions; new /api/session/{id}/wait ('Wait for a session agent loop to become idle'), /interrupt, /prompt, /model, /agent, /compact, /permission, /question, GET /api/session/active ('foreground Session drains owned by this process'); POST /experimental/session/{id}/background = 'Detach any synchronous subagents currently blocking the session and continue them in the background'. Kilo 7.2.20 (installed, several releases behind 7.8.8) serves a 7-path /doc, so the same routes are NOT confirmed for Kilo. Not probed: a model-backed run (no provider credentials were used), so the blocking is read from the schema, not observed in a live task
data.question: How do subagents, parallel sessions and steering behave in opencode 1.19.0, probed on the real binary?

data.body: Falsifiable claims with a recorded probe each, Claude Code and Kilo first (both installed here), the rest from source and docs: (1) Kilo's task/subagent tool blocks the parent until the child session ends (operator-observed, mechanism unverified), while a second session via kilo serve plus prompt_async does not; (2) Claude Agent run_in_background returns at once and notifies on completion, SendMessage continues; (3) Codex spawn_agent: does it return immediately, how are messages sent to the agent, how is the result read; (4) Gemini subagents; (5) Cursor and Antigravity background agents; (6) Copilot cloud delegation; (7) Cline spawn/team. Each result lands in the descriptor's [spawn] section as data (blocking yes/no/unknown, background, steer, resume, abort, result retrieval, depth, isolation) with source and date. Unknown stays unknown. OPENCODE (added 2026-10-12): treat opencode 1.19 and Kilo as ONE engine family (Kilo is an opencode v1 fork; descriptor family = opencode) and probe once for both: the task/subagent tool's blocking behaviour, `opencode serve` + `opencode run --attach` / POST /session + prompt_async + /abort + GET /event for independent sessions, `opencode run -s/--fork/--share`, parallel sessions under one server. Differences to record separately: opencode lacks Kilo-only features (agent_manager tool, /goal, wakeup tools, session.turn events); opencode V2 (dev branch, 2.0.27) has an incompatible plugin and possibly different session API, so every [spawn] value for opencode carries a version range and the adapter is version-gated (opencode --version major 1 vs 2). PROBED 2026-10-12 (R-spawn-opencode-probe, opencode 1.19.0 installed in a scratch dir, isolated HOME): subagents are SYNCHRONOUS by default (the schema of POST /experimental/session/{id}/background says 'Detach any synchronous subagents currently blocking the session and continue them in the background'); subagents are child sessions (GET /session/{id}/children); parallel sessions under one server work; abort, interrupt, wait, prompt_async, /session/status and /api/session/active exist; `opencode acp` is an ACP server. Still to probe: the same routes on Kilo 7.8.x (installed 7.2.20 is too old to show them), and a model-backed run to OBSERVE the blocking (needs a provider credential the operator supplies).

ddflow spawn steer|pause|resume|cancel|rescope <lane>: steer sends a message the child sees next (Kilo prompt_async queues while busy; Claude SendMessage; Codex message to the agent; ACP prompt where used; otherwise a lane.note the child receives through its change feed and the hook doors), pause and cancel abort the turn (Kilo abort endpoint, process signal for launched lanes) and keep or release the lease, resume restarts with the hand-off, rescope edits the item (globs, body, safeguards) and the child is told. Every verb is logged, a master may steer only its own children unless the operator says otherwise, and a harness that cannot do one says so (parity report). opencode/Kilo mechanics (probed on opencode 1.19.0): steer = POST /session/{id}/prompt_async (queues while busy), cancel = POST /session/{id}/abort or POST /api/session/{id}/interrupt, wait = POST /api/session/{id}/wait, state = GET /session/status and GET /api/session/active, children = GET /session/{id}/children, fork = POST /session/{id}/fork.

NAMING (2026-10-12): `ddflow lanes` (B-gap-lanes) is the READ-ONLY ledger and advisor of lanes: it lists lanes, their state and the exact spawn line, and never spawns. This task adds the ACTING side under a different command and module: `ddflow launch` (services/launcher.py, declared/launch.py, [launch] knobs). Listing and showing lanes is the ledger's job (`ddflow lanes`); launch verbs read it, they do not duplicate it. Needs B-gap-lanes. ddflow launch start|stop|resume|steer <agent> [--item ID] [--model M] [--effort E]; one supervisor over ddflow job run (detached, survives the caller), a worktree and lease per lane, the session id captured and recorded, the JSON/event stream parsed into ddflow events, heartbeats from it, the continuation engine deciding re-invocation (claude -p --resume, codex exec resume, opencode run -s, kilo run -s / kilo serve + prompt_async, gemini -p, grok -p --resume, cline --id, aider --message loop). Safety: launch templates and permission flags are operator-set (local layer or allowlist); a cloned project cannot add a launcher; credentials only from the environment; spend and turn caps from knobs. It is also the piece the governor's restart-on-tier (P-governor.actions), B-ac-smoke, agent caps slots (P-agent-caps) and remote management use. Reuses jobs, worktrees, leases, quota; no second process manager. ACP (verified 2026-10-12): `opencode acp` starts an Agent Client Protocol server, so ACP is one more launch template type for opencode; the server route (opencode serve + attach/prompt_async) is the other.

When the master is blocked waiting for a synchronous subagent (the opencode and Kilo default), the user or another door can run ddflow spawn detach [--session S]: for opencode 1.x it calls POST /experimental/session/{id}/background on the session's server (needs the server address: a ddflow plugin records it, or the session was started by the launcher), after which the child continues as a background lane the ledger shows and the master is free. Descriptor [spawn.native] detach = {route}. Where a harness has no detach, say so and offer abort (steer) or the independent-session route. Version-gated and experimental-flagged (the route is under /experimental): a failing call never harms the session. A plugin hook can also call it automatically after N minutes of a blocking child ([spawn] auto_detach_after_s, off by default).

data.body: Closes B-hy-kilo-onboard (extend it, do not duplicate). A .kilo/plugin/ddflow.ts (and the opencode equivalent) that: calls ddflow hooks run for chat.message (prompt capture), tool.execute.before (throw to block, as probed on 7.2.20) and after (monitoring), shell.env (session id), experimental.session.compacting (handoff), and on root-session session.idle asks the continuation engine and calls client.session.promptAsync with the next prompt (cap, abort/error/child-session tracking, loop guard). Guards: opencode 2.x has an incompatible plugin API (detect the version, do not install a broken plugin, say so); verified on Kilo CLI and the VS Code extension (shared engine); a plugin-free fallback is the lane launcher over kilo serve. Probe the unverified parts on Kilo 7.8.8: idle ordering, abort versus completion. OPENCODE V2 (R-opencode-v2, probed 2026-10-12): the gate is on the PLUGIN only. The v2 dev build serves the same 162 HTTP paths as 1.19.0, so the server route (serve, attach, prompt_async, abort, wait, background) is version-agnostic and is the default for opencode; the in-process plugin is the 1.x implementation, and a v2 implementation is P-agent-parity.opencode-v2.

Falsifiable claims with a recorded probe each, Claude Code and Kilo first (both installed here), the rest from source and docs: (1) Kilo's task/subagent tool blocks the parent until the child session ends (operator-observed, mechanism unverified), while a second session via kilo serve plus prompt_async does not; (2) Claude Agent run_in_background returns at once and notifies on completion, SendMessage continues; (3) Codex spawn_agent: does it return immediately, how are messages sent to the agent, how is the result read; (4) Gemini subagents; (5) Cursor and Antigravity background agents; (6) Copilot cloud delegation; (7) Cline spawn/team. Each result lands in the descriptor's [spawn] section as data (blocking yes/no/unknown, background, steer, resume, abort, result retrieval, depth, isolation) with source and date. Unknown stays unknown. OPENCODE (added 2026-10-12): treat opencode 1.19 and Kilo as ONE engine family (Kilo is an opencode v1 fork; descriptor family = opencode) and probe once for both: the task/subagent tool's blocking behaviour, `opencode serve` + `opencode run --attach` / POST /session + prompt_async + /abort + GET /event for independent sessions, `opencode run -s/--fork/--share`, parallel sessions under one server. Differences to record separately: opencode lacks Kilo-only features (agent_manager tool, /goal, wakeup tools, session.turn events); opencode V2 (dev branch, 2.0.27) has an incompatible plugin and possibly different session API, so every [spawn] value for opencode carries a version range and the adapter is version-gated (opencode --version major 1 vs 2). PROBED 2026-10-12 (R-spawn-opencode-probe, opencode 1.19.0 installed in a scratch dir, isolated HOME): subagents are SYNCHRONOUS by default (the schema of POST /experimental/session/{id}/background says 'Detach any synchronous subagents currently blocking the session and continue them in the background'); subagents are child sessions (GET /session/{id}/children); parallel sessions under one server work; abort, interrupt, wait, prompt_async, /session/status and /api/session/active exist; `opencode acp` is an ACP server. Still to probe: the same routes on Kilo 7.8.x (installed 7.2.20 is too old to show them), and a model-backed run to OBSERVE the blocking (needs a provider credential the operator supplies). V2: the opencode dev build (0.0.0-dev-202610110139) has the same session routes (background, prompt_async, abort, interrupt, wait, children) as 1.19.0, so spawn, steer and detach need no V2 gate; only the plugin differs.

The opencode V2 plugin API (Plugin.define({id, setup(ctx)}), hooks under ctx.session.hook('prompt'|'context'|'compaction'|...)) replaces the v1 named hooks. Write the V2 implementation of the ddflow plugin (prompt capture, tool monitoring and enforcement, session id, handoff on compaction, stop-to-continue through the continuation engine) behind the same contract as the 1.x one, selected by 'opencode --version'; until V2 is the npm latest it is opt-in. A weekly matrix job (P-agent-parity.drift) installs the latest, dev, next and beta tags into a scratch dir with an isolated HOME and runs the no-credential probes: server paths still present (the 162-path comparison), plugin loads, hook names; a change is a drift alert before users hit it. The server route needs no V2 gate (R-opencode-v2). Needs a plugin-loading probe that was NOT done on 2026-10-12.
data.title: opencode V2: a second plugin implementation and a compatibility matrix across the latest, dev, next and beta builds

data.claim: ddflow already holds the raw material (an event log with case ids, states, agents and timestamps, plus doctor notes, gate rates, flake detection, cadence misses, the adaptive flow controller and a planned metrics service) and the delivery channels (jobs, triggers, a proposal record in P-goals, change feeds), but nothing joins them into detect, interpret, propose, apply and measure: detection is scattered notes with no finding record, no LLM retrospective with verification exists, proposals are not typed or applicable, there are no phase-boundary moments, and no bounded experiment loop; the log is a process-mining event log, so conformance and bottleneck analysis can be deterministic, with the LLM used for interpretation and proposals that must cite evidence and survive a cross-family check
data.falsifier: the existing log cannot answer where time goes per item (state durations, rework, waits), or a cross-family model's improvement proposals cannot be checked against the log
data.mechanism: events carry item, state change, agent and time; gate.* events give yield and duration; lease and claim events give lock waits (claim refusals are NOT logged today); doctor emits ad hoc notes (gate_flapping, duplicate_work, cadence behind, flaky test, orphan worktrees); services/rates.py measures gate fire rates and cadence hit rates; flowstate samples signals for the AIMD controller; B-prop-model/B-prop-discover plan a proposal record and a periodic discovery job; schedule jobs and triggers create items; lessons, decisions and rules are the memory an analysis needs
data.probe: inventory: doctor note kinds, services/rates.py, flowstate/flowcontrol, ddflow loops, cadence passes, the open tasks of P-goals (B-prop-*, B-goal-report, B-goal-eval), P-schedule (B-sched-run, B-trigger-*), P-gaps (B-gap-metrics), P-lessons, P-governor, P-change-surface.footprint; doctor on this repo; forced-completion repair found 12 deviations from the defined pipeline at upgrade
data.probe_output: doctor note kinds seen: gate_flapping (13), duplicate_work (3), cadence behind (2), flaky test (1), orphan_worktree (59), embedder; the upgrade repair found 12 items completed with --force over unmet gates, i.e. conformance checking against the defined pipeline already finds real deviations; no finding record, no claim.refused event, no phase.started/research.completed trigger source, no typed proposal, no experiment loop; B-prop-model (proposal record, person-only adopt/defer/reject), B-prop-discover (disabled-by-default periodic discovery) and B-goal-report (acceptance rate) are open; others (from general knowledge, not freshly surveyed): process mining and conformance checking on event logs, DORA and flow metrics (cycle time, WIP, throughput), SRE postmortems and error budgets, Kaizen retrospectives, AIOps anomaly detection, LLM self-improvement research (Reflexion, Voyager skill library, Agent Workflow Memory, DSPy and TextGrad prompt optimisation, self-modifying agents), and their known failure modes (Goodhart, LLM-as-judge self-preference, feedback loops)
data.question: How can ddflow observe itself and each project's workflow, with the help of the LLM and the agents, find defects, inefficiency and deviations, propose improvements at the right moments, and optimise itself safely?

data.body: Operator 2026-10-12: ddflow should self-monitor and self-observe, with the help of the LLM and agents, detect bugs, defects, inefficiency and deviations per project workflow, propose improvements (to the project, the way of work and the workflow) when research ends, when a phase starts or ends, and periodically, and optimise itself: workflow, quality, cost. Research R-observe (CONFIRMED). Reuses and extends, not duplicates: P-goals (B-prop-model proposal record, B-prop-discover periodic discovery, B-goal-report acceptance numbers), P-schedule (jobs, triggers, escalation), P-gaps (B-gap-metrics), B-adaptive-flow (the AIMD pattern), P-governor (tier feedback), P-lessons (effect), P-safeguards (cost), P-change-surface (footprint), P-coherence (contradictions), P-configurable (logged config changes). Principles: deterministic detection first, the LLM interprets and proposes with cited evidence and a cross-family check, the operator decides, auto-tuning only inside operator-set bounds with automatic rollback, everything logged, every number a knob.
data.title: Self-observation and self-improvement: detect, interpret with the LLM, propose at the right moments, apply within bounds, measure the effect

data.body: Coordinator-only. Proposal: levels observe < propose < tune-within-bounds, default propose; an allowlist of auto-tunable knobs with min, max, step and rate limit (everything else proposal-only); retrospectives run by a cross-family reviewer endpoint within a token budget (knobs); no cross-project data leaves the machine by default; only the operator accepts workflow, rule and safeguard proposals, agents may accept their own task-scoped ones. Blocked until the operator answers.
data.title: Operator decisions: autonomy level, which knobs may self-tune, LLM budget for retrospectives, privacy and cross-project sharing, who accepts proposals

data.reason: operator decision on autonomy, bounds, budget and privacy

data.body: What cannot be seen today: a refused claim and why (lock waits) is not an event; time waiting for the operator (approvals, questions) is not measured; tool-call and idle time per lane live only in the transcripts (P-agent-memory capture); review and gate cost is spread over events. Add the few missing events (claim.refused with the blocking item and glob, ask.waited when the ask engine exists) with upcasters, and derived views for per-item state durations, queue wait, rework (reopen, gate re-run, review rounds), lane starvation. ddflow observe signals lists every signal, its source and its freshness; an unreadable signal is UNAVAILABLE, never zero. Reuses B-gap-metrics for the replay.
data.title: Close the telemetry gaps: claim refusals, human-wait time, per-state durations, rework, gate and review cost as events or derived views, with a list of signals and their freshness

data.body: Each detector is a pure function over a log slice (one small module each, registered by convention): state-duration bottleneck (p90 by state and phase), rework loops, gate yield (never fails, always fails, flapping, cost per catch: a gate that never catches anything is a candidate to skip for small changes), hot-file lock contention from refused claims (P-change-surface.footprint), lanes idle while work is ready, item aging, forecast error (B-gap-metrics), cadence misses (services/rates.py), cost outliers by tier (B-gap-spend), repeated bug classes (P-lessons.recurrence), plan lint defects, slow tests, card drift (P-safeguards.drift-check). Thresholds are knobs; no LLM; a detector that cannot run is UNAVAILABLE.
data.title: Deterministic detectors as a registry: bottlenecks, rework loops, gate yield, lock contention, idle lanes, aging, estimate error, cadence misses, cost outliers, drift, plan defects

data.body: Process-mining style: replay each item's trace against its effective pipeline and rules (ddflow verify already does part of it per item) and report deviations as findings with the item, the rule and the agent. The upgrade repair already found 12 items completed with --force over unmet gates, so the signal is real. Deviations an operator waived (task-scoped waivers, recorded overrides) are not findings. Per-project: the defined workflow is the project's own config.
data.title: Conformance checking: the log versus the workflow the project DEFINED (forced completions, skipped required gates, same-family reviews, late bug filing, missing lessons, unverified passes)

data.body: A finding kind on the shared RecordKind descriptor (list, show, dismiss, reopen, history): id by detector and key, severity, scope, evidence (event ids and a digest, no text), first and last seen, trend, status. ddflow insights [--scope] on CLI and MCP; doctor lists the top N; the brief carries at most three lines (knob). Dismissing records the reason and suppresses re-raising until the evidence materially changes; findings that stay open and unseen age into a digest instead of nagging.
data.title: The finding record and ddflow insights: stored, deduplicated, trended, dismissible with a reason, shown in doctor and a budgeted brief line

data.body: ddflow retro run [--scope project|phase|week] renders an overridable prompt with the findings digest, relevant decisions, lessons and safeguards, and bounded log slices, and sends it to a reviewer endpoint of a DIFFERENT model family than the working agents (reviewers machinery) or files it as a research item for an agent (B-sched-run). The output must be structured: observation, cited finding and event ids, hypothesis, proposed change, expected metric effect, risk, falsifier. A verifier re-derives every cited number and event from the log; an unsupported claim is kept but marked THEORETICAL, never proposed as fact. Output is fenced data. Knobs: model endpoint, token budget per run, slices, cadence. Honest limit: LLM-as-judge bias is why the checker is deterministic.
data.title: The retrospective agent: an LLM reads the findings and bounded log slices and proposes improvements with cited evidence and a falsifier; every claim is checked

data.body: Extends B-prop-model (the proposal record with person-only adopt, defer, reject) with a TYPED change set: config_change{key, from, to, bounds}, workflow_change{pipeline or gate edit, previewed with ddflow workflow preview}, add_rule/safeguard/lesson/card, file_task, install_companion, process_note; each with expected metric, risk, rollback and, where it is a tunable, an experiment design. Accepting applies it through the owning verb (config set, rule add, task add) with provenance (proposal id in the config.changed event); rejecting or deferring records the reason, which suppresses similar proposals. A plain-prompt review ('show me the proposals') and bulk accept of the cheap ones. Proposals expire.
data.title: Typed proposals that can be applied: config change, workflow change, rule or safeguard or lesson, task to file, companion install; with predicted effect, risk and rollback

data.body: New trigger sources: research.completed, phase.started (first claim in a phase), phase.completed; shipped jobs, each a knob, cheap deterministic ones on, LLM ones off by default: (1) research completed -> 'what does this change in the plan' (affected open tasks, decisions to revisit, new tasks); (2) phase start -> pre-flight: plan lint, capacity forecast, parallelism suggestion, related lessons and risks, suggested order; (3) phase end -> retro: metrics versus forecast, deviations, lesson candidates, process proposals; (4) weekly workflow review and monthly deep audit; (5) event triggers (cost spike, flapping gate, stall, repeated refusal). Noise control: max proposals per week, dedupe, cooldown, digest instead of interruption (B-sched-escalation).
data.title: Proposals at the right moments: research completed, phase start (pre-flight), phase end (retro), periodic, and on events like a cost spike or flapping gate

data.body: For knobs the operator marks auto (min, max, step, rate limit per knob family; one experiment at a time per family): a trial by alternating assignment per item (hash) or before/after windows, with guardrails (gate failure rate, rework, post-merge bugs, cost, time-to-complete), a pre-registered window and sample size, a stop rule, and automatic rollback when a guardrail breaches. Continuous knobs may reuse the AIMD controller of B-adaptive-flow. Every step is a config.changed event with the experiment id; results are findings. Default: no knob is auto; proposals only. Candidate knobs: review.max_rounds, gates.unit_tests_small_lines, review.combined_under_lines, lessons.max_results, the governor ladder marks, context budgets. Guard against Goodhart: guardrails are measured independently of the target.
data.title: Bounded self-optimisation: allowlisted knobs, controlled trials with guardrail metrics, pre-registered stop rules and automatic rollback; off by default

data.body: ddflow insights effect: for each applied proposal the metric before and after against its prediction, whether it was reversed, tokens spent producing it; per detector and proposal type, hit rate (accepted and helped / raised). Detectors and proposal types that never help are muted by default and listed for retirement; the observer's own cost is budgeted (knob) and reported next to its yield. Small numbers are reported as such (no false precision). Feeds B-goal-report.
data.title: Close the loop: did an accepted proposal help? predicted versus actual, reversal rate, cost of observing, and which detectors and proposal types earn their keep

data.body: R-observe lists the field from general knowledge, not a fresh survey. Do the survey from primary sources: process mining and conformance on event logs (pm4py style), DORA and flow metrics, SRE postmortems and error budgets, agent self-improvement work (Reflexion, Voyager, Agent Workflow Memory, DSPy and TextGrad, self-modifying agents) and what coding-agent products and orchestrators ship for retrospectives and analytics. Output: which ideas to adopt, which failure modes (Goodhart, judge bias, runaway optimisation) to design against, with sources, dates and confidence. Verdict may change task bodies in this phase.
data.title: Research: what comparable tools and the self-improvement literature actually do, and what they got wrong

data.body: Falsifiable claim: the same detectors run on ddflow, home-simulator and run_nemo_run give comparable numbers that justify different defaults per project type. Probe on the three local logs (read-only). Privacy: numbers only, no text, redaction profile, explicit opt-in, nothing leaves the machine by default. Verdict decides whether any build task is filed.
data.title: Research (opt-in, later): anonymised aggregate statistics across projects to seed better defaults and compare workflows

data.body: A shipped /improve command and MCP prompt: summarises the open findings and proposals for the current scope in a few lines, shows the evidence behind each, lets the user accept, defer or reject by sentence; also /retro to run one now. Works on every harness that has MCP prompts or commands, with an instruction-text fallback.
data.title: Plain prompts: 'what should we improve?' and 'run a retro' with the evidence, the proposals and a yes/no per proposal

data.body: A throwaway project with a seeded log (a bottleneck state, a flapping gate, a forced completion, a hot file with refused claims, an idle lane with ready work): the detectors raise exactly those findings; a fake reviewer returns one proposal with a wrong cited number (marked THEORETICAL) and one correct (applied through config set with provenance); a phase-end retro fires once and respects the weekly cap; a trial with a breaching guardrail rolls back automatically; a dismissed finding stays quiet until its evidence changes; CLI and MCP bodies are identical.
data.title: Acceptance: seeded inefficiencies are detected, an LLM retro proposes with checked evidence, a proposal is applied, a trial rolls back on a guardrail breach, all logged

data.mechanism: shipped: job definitions in the log, .ddflow/schedules/*.toml or [cadence] with validation (schedule.defined/updated/removed), event triggers in .ddflow/triggers/*.toml with window, debounce, cooldown, dedupe key, hop limit, breaker and a global cap, firing creates a queue item from a job template and never starts an agent (D-trigger-actions-create-items), and ddflow cadence for count passes; D-sched-no-daemon means due-ness is computed from the log and something else must start it; planned and open: B-sched-due (calendar due), B-sched-run (run a due job, file items), B-sched-author (CLI and one MCP tool), B-sched-emitters (cron, systemd, Actions snippets and a doctor warning for a silent no-fire), B-sched-defaults (security, dependency, architecture, duplication, CI-health jobs), B-trigger-events and B-trigger-defaults, B-sched-escalation

data.probe_output: ddflow has no schedule or trigger command (ddflow --help lists cadence only); ddflow cadence shows only DUE integration_tests and dedupe_sweep by task count (749 tasks since last); calendar every_days jobs are defined but nothing evaluates them (B-sched-due open); no task starts an agent to work the queue unattended (the launcher is P-agent-parity.launcher); the only upstream watch is ddflow's own release check (B-upgrade.8, done) and bespoke planned checks (P-agent-parity.drift, companions listing); P-schedule is 4/16 and waits for the docs wave
data.question: Can ddflow run periodic and event-triggered work per project, fully managed by the user, for full-suite checks (duplication, bugs, security), dependency and partner-tool updates, and for ddflow itself keeping up with the coding agents?

data.body: R-schedule-reach: nothing watches partner tools, dependencies or the coding agents generically. A watch is a definition (.ddflow/watches/<id>.toml, log events like schedules, same validation and authoring verbs): source, how to read the current value, how to compare with the last seen, the job whose template files the item, a minimum interval, enabled. State is the last seen value, kept as watch.observed events so it replays and merges. A change files an item from the job template with the before/after and links; no change files nothing; an unreachable source is UNAVAILABLE and counted (a watch that is silent for N periods is itself a doctor note). Network use is operator-defined: allowed hosts are an operator-only knob; nothing is fetched from a committed config the operator did not approve. Rate limits and offline behaviour are knobs.
data.title: Watches: a generic upstream-change primitive (version, changelog, release feed, command output) that files research or upgrade items when something changes

data.body: One small module per source, registered by convention: npm, PyPI, crates.io, GitHub releases and tags, Docker tags, an installed tool's --version and --help digest (the agent CLIs, companions), the project's own outdated report (uv pip list --outdated, npm outdated, cargo outdated, go list -u), a changelog or docs page by content digest or feed. Each returns a value, a digest and a retrieved time; a failure says why. No credential in a committed file; keys from the environment only. Tests use recorded fixtures and a fake server, never the network.
data.title: Watch source adapters: package indexes, release feeds, installed CLI versions, lockfile outdated reports, changelog pages

data.body: Keeping up with an upstream tool is research, then a decision, then work. A chain template files the research item on a change (what changed, what it means for this project, a falsifiable claim and a probe), and on its completion a proposal or implementation tasks (P-observe.proposals), and a verification item (the live smoke or the conformance run) once those land. Stages are linked items, so the lease, gates and cross-family review apply to each; a chain has a budget and a cap on open stages; it never starts an agent by itself (D-trigger-actions-create-items).
data.title: Multi-stage jobs: watch -> research item -> adoption proposal -> verification, each stage an ordinary item with its own pipeline

data.body: D-sched-no-daemon means due-ness is computed but something else must start the work. An executor is registered per project (ddflow schedule executor add): a harness routine (Claude Code Routines, cron or /loop), an OpenClaw cron or heartbeat, a GitHub Actions workflow, a systemd timer or plain cron; the emitter prints exactly what to install (B-sched-emitters) and the executor's heartbeat is recorded so doctor can say 'job X was due 3 days ago and no executor has run' (the silent no-fire failure). The executor runs ddflow schedule due --run and then works the filed items through the lane launcher headless (P-agent-parity.launcher) with an unattended permission profile, spend and turn caps, quota guard (P-governor) and the operator's approval for merges of dependency, security and architecture changes. Report-only is the default mode.
data.title: Who works the queue when nobody is there: register an executor, emit its schedule, run headless with caps, and warn when a job is due and nothing will run it

data.body: Extends B-sched-defaults (security, dependency, architecture, duplication, CI health, SECURITY.md sync) with a catalogue chosen per project type (Python, JS, Rust, Go, ML repo): full-suite duplication sweep, whole-codebase bug audit, security audit and advisory check, dependency updates (grouped, never auto-merged), licence check, secret scan, dead code, doc freshness and link check, flaky-test quarantine, slow-test report, coverage trend, log backup verify, agent-config drift, release readiness. Every entry is data (a job plus a prompt), disabled by default except cheap report-only ones, and edited, disabled or deleted by the user with the same verbs; ddflow schedule init offers the set for the detected project type with the cost and frequency of each.
data.title: A library of project-type job templates chosen at onboarding: duplication, bug audit, security, dependencies, licences, secrets, dead code, doc freshness and links, flaky and slow tests, coverage, backup, agent-config drift

data.body: The concrete definitions this repository runs on itself (a project can copy them): a weekly watch over every supported agent CLI (--version, --help digest, release feed) that files a research item per change with the descriptor to re-verify; a monthly market re-scan for new agents; companion versions (roborev, codeguide, context7, memory); MCP spec and SDK versions; Python, uv, ruff and CI action versions; each chain ends in descriptor corrections, new parity features or a closed 'nothing to do' with the reason. P-agent-parity.drift becomes the agent-specific checks on top of this machinery, not a separate scheduler.
data.title: ddflow's own upkeep set: coding-agent updates and new features, companion and partner tools, protocol versions, runtime and tooling, as watches and chains

data.body: ddflow schedule history [id]: runs, outcome (ok, findings, failed, unavailable, budget-hit), items and bugs filed, duration, tokens or spend where known, and the yield (findings per run, accepted per filed). A job with zero yield over N runs is flagged and a slower cadence proposed (P-observe.proposals), a job that always finds something is flagged for a fix task; the circuit breaker of B-sched-run is the hard stop, this is the soft signal. Feeds P-observe.effect.
data.title: Job outcomes and yield: history, cost and findings per run, and a frequency suggestion when a job never finds anything

data.body: Extends B-sched-author with what a user needs day to day: ddflow schedule next shows the coming runs with an estimated cost (from history), snooze until a date, skip this occurrence, run now, quiet hours and a project time zone as knobs (a due run waits for the window), per-job and per-week run budgets, and a plain-prompt route ('run the security audit every Monday, report only') that shows the definition before saving. The same verbs for watches and triggers; every change is logged (D-everything-configurable) and an agent-added job starts disabled.
data.title: Manage by command and by prompt: list, show, edit, enable, disable, snooze, skip, run now, preview the next runs and cost, quiet hours and time zones

data.body: doctor and harness verify compare each installed agent's version with the descriptor's verified version and flag a newer one; shipped schedules (knobs): weekly --help and changelog diff for tier-1 agents, monthly market re-scan, quarterly tier review; fixture re-record (B-ac-fixtures) when a hook or MCP schema changed; opencode 2.x and Antigravity-style config moves are caught as drift before users hit them. REUSE (2026-10-12): the scheduling of these checks is NOT built here: the weekly agent watches and the monthly market re-scan are definitions on P-schedule.watch / P-schedule.chain / P-schedule.ddflow-set; this task keeps the agent-specific checks (descriptor version comparison, fixture re-record, plugin-load probes).

data.text: Ask me the questions

Answers (AskUserQuestion, 2026-10-13): P-observe autonomy = propose plus bounded auto-tuning from the start; retro model = both compared (cross-family endpoint and the working agent); schedule order = yes, authoring/calendar due/run/watch/executor before the docs wave; probe = try a free anonymous model first

data.decision: Operator 2026-10-13 (AskUserQuestion). (1) AUTONOMY: ddflow detects and proposes, and may also TUNE BOUNDED KNOBS from the start: an allowlist with min, max, step and a rate limit per knob family, one experiment at a time per family, guardrail metrics measured independently of the target, a pre-registered window and stop rule, and automatic rollback when a guardrail breaches; every step is a config.changed event with the experiment id. Everything outside the allowlist is proposal-only and needs the operator; workflow, rule and safeguard proposals are accepted only by the operator (an agent may accept its own task-scoped ones). Initial allowlist, all editable by the operator: review.max_rounds, review.combined_under_lines, gates.unit_tests_small_lines, lessons.max_results, the context budgets, the governor ladder marks. (2) RETROSPECTIVES run on BOTH a different-family reviewer endpoint and the working agent, and the two are compared: where they disagree is reported, a proposal both make carries more weight, and each run is budgeted (token budget per run, weekly cap: knobs). (3) Not asked, defaults: no cross-project data leaves the machine; LLM-run moments are off until the operator enables them, cheap deterministic ones are on. All values are knobs (D-everything-configurable).
data.title: Self-observation: propose plus bounded auto-tuning from the start; retrospectives run by both a cross-family model and the working agent, compared

data.was: operator decision on autonomy, bounds, budget and privacy

data.reason: done as a decision: D-observe (accepted 2026-10-13)

data.decision: Operator 2026-10-13: B-sched-author, B-sched-due, B-sched-run, B-sched-emitters, P-schedule.watch, P-schedule.watch-sources and a basic executor are ordered AHEAD of the docs wave (D-old-work-behind-core-docs is amended for these tasks only). The rest of P-schedule (library, ddflow-set, outcomes, manage, chain, defaults, flaky, compaction, escalation, docs) stays behind the docs wave. The FULL unattended executor (headless runs through the lane launcher, caps, quota guard) needs P-agent-parity.launcher and stays where that lands; the BASIC executor (register a harness routine, cron or GitHub Actions line; heartbeat; doctor warning when a due job has no executor) needs no launcher and comes early.
data.title: Periodic work comes before the docs wave: authoring, calendar due, run, watch and a basic executor

data.body: No launcher needed. ddflow schedule executor add --kind routine|cron|actions|systemd|openclaw|loop prints exactly what to install (B-sched-emitters); the executor's prompt or script runs ddflow schedule due --run and then works the filed items in an ordinary agent session; each run records a heartbeat (schedule.executor.ran) so doctor says 'job X was due 3 days ago and no executor has run it' (the silent no-fire failure: Actions disables idle schedules after 60 days, /loop expires after 7 days). The headless, capped, quota-guarded version is P-schedule.unattended.
data.title: Basic executor: register how due jobs get started, emit it, heartbeat it, and warn when a job is due and nothing runs it

data.claim: In opencode 1.19.0 the task tool runs the subagent as a child session and the parent stays busy until the child finishes (blocking); the documented detach route did not free it in this setup; aborting the child does free the parent immediately
data.falsifier: the parent goes idle while the child still runs, or the detach route frees the parent
data.mechanism: task tool creates a child session observable at GET /session/{id}/children; /session/status shows the parent busy for the child's whole run; POST /experimental/session/{id}/background is documented to detach blocking subagents; POST /session/{child}/abort stops the child
data.probe: opencode-ai 1.19.0 in a scratch directory with isolated HOME; opencode serve --pure; free anonymous model opencode/big-pickle (no credential); a parent session prompted via prompt_async to use the task tool once for a subagent running 'sleep 35'; polled /session/status and /session/{id}/children every 2 s; run 1 called POST /experimental/session/{id}/background 8 s after the child appeared; run 2 called POST /session/{child}/abort; run 3 called POST /api/session/{parent}/interrupt
data.probe_output: run 1: child session appeared at 6 s, parent stayed busy from 2 s to 44 s, detach call at 14 s returned (200, false) and changed nothing, parent went idle at 46 s right after the child finished, final assistant text FINISHED; run 2: abort of the child returned (200, true) and both parent and child were idle within 2 s (the parent's turn ended too); run 3: INCONCLUSIVE (the model never started a child in that run, so interrupt was not exercised); my sleep-process counter was unreliable (it counted its own pgrep) and is discarded; free models listed without credentials: opencode/big-pickle, nemotron-3.5-lightning-free, ling-3.1-flash-free and others; Kilo not probed model-backed (installed 7.2.20 too old)
data.question: Does opencode 1.19.0 really block the parent session while a subagent runs, and which routes free it?

data.body: Falsifiable claims with a recorded probe each, Claude Code and Kilo first (both installed here), the rest from source and docs: (1) Kilo's task/subagent tool blocks the parent until the child session ends (operator-observed, mechanism unverified), while a second session via kilo serve plus prompt_async does not; (2) Claude Agent run_in_background returns at once and notifies on completion, SendMessage continues; (3) Codex spawn_agent: does it return immediately, how are messages sent to the agent, how is the result read; (4) Gemini subagents; (5) Cursor and Antigravity background agents; (6) Copilot cloud delegation; (7) Cline spawn/team. Each result lands in the descriptor's [spawn] section as data (blocking yes/no/unknown, background, steer, resume, abort, result retrieval, depth, isolation) with source and date. Unknown stays unknown. OPENCODE (added 2026-10-12): treat opencode 1.19 and Kilo as ONE engine family (Kilo is an opencode v1 fork; descriptor family = opencode) and probe once for both: the task/subagent tool's blocking behaviour, `opencode serve` + `opencode run --attach` / POST /session + prompt_async + /abort + GET /event for independent sessions, `opencode run -s/--fork/--share`, parallel sessions under one server. Differences to record separately: opencode lacks Kilo-only features (agent_manager tool, /goal, wakeup tools, session.turn events); opencode V2 (dev branch, 2.0.27) has an incompatible plugin and possibly different session API, so every [spawn] value for opencode carries a version range and the adapter is version-gated (opencode --version major 1 vs 2). PROBED 2026-10-12 (R-spawn-opencode-probe, opencode 1.19.0 installed in a scratch dir, isolated HOME): subagents are SYNCHRONOUS by default (the schema of POST /experimental/session/{id}/background says 'Detach any synchronous subagents currently blocking the session and continue them in the background'); subagents are child sessions (GET /session/{id}/children); parallel sessions under one server work; abort, interrupt, wait, prompt_async, /session/status and /api/session/active exist; `opencode acp` is an ACP server. Still to probe: the same routes on Kilo 7.8.x (installed 7.2.20 is too old to show them), and a model-backed run to OBSERVE the blocking (needs a provider credential the operator supplies). V2: the opencode dev build (0.0.0-dev-202610110139) has the same session routes (background, prompt_async, abort, interrupt, wait, children) as 1.19.0, so spawn, steer and detach need no V2 gate; only the plugin differs. OBSERVED 2026-10-13 (R-opencode-blocking-observed, free model, no credential): the opencode task tool BLOCKS the parent (busy 2 s to 44 s while the child ran 6 s to ~44 s); POST /experimental/session/{id}/background returned false and freed nothing; POST /session/{child}/abort freed the parent in about 2 s (its turn ended). Interrupt of the parent was not exercised. Kilo is still unprobed model-backed.

When the master is blocked waiting for a synchronous subagent (the opencode and Kilo default), the user or another door can run ddflow spawn detach [--session S]: for opencode 1.x it calls POST /experimental/session/{id}/background on the session's server (needs the server address: a ddflow plugin records it, or the session was started by the launcher), after which the child continues as a background lane the ledger shows and the master is free. Descriptor [spawn.native] detach = {route}. Where a harness has no detach, say so and offer abort (steer) or the independent-session route. Version-gated and experimental-flagged (the route is under /experimental): a failing call never harms the session. A plugin hook can also call it automatically after N minutes of a blocking child ([spawn] auto_detach_after_s, off by default). PROBE RESULT (R-opencode-blocking-observed): the experimental background route returned false on opencode 1.19.0 and did not detach, so it is NOT relied on: the verb tries it first (cheap, harmless) and then falls back to the verified route: POST /session/{child}/abort frees the parent within about 2 s; the child's work is then re-run as an independent lane (P-spawn.engine) with the same brief. Need to learn why the route returns false (a required experimental flag, or only valid from the TUI) before promising detach; that is the first step of this task.
data.title: Unblock a stuck master: ddflow spawn unblock frees a parent blocked on a subagent (detach where it works, otherwise cancel the child and relaunch it as an independent lane)

data.body: The driver and the MCP instructions say: delegate with ddflow spawn, not with a blocking subagent tool, for anything that may take more than a few minutes; do not sit in ddflow wait; check lanes or wait for the notice. harness verify flags a harness whose only native route blocks (Kilo's task tool, per the facts) and names the independent-session route. Honest limit: where a model ignores the instruction ddflow cannot stop it; the parity suite measures it. Evidence: opencode 1.19.0 task tool observed blocking the parent for the child's whole run; for long delegations use the independent-session route.
