data.claim: The plan covers three things well: record changes reaching a running session through the doors its harness calls (B-rc-changes, B-rc-context), hand-off and fork between sessions and harnesses (B-sc-transfer), and the session tree and native lane status; it does not cover directed, live context: a message from the master or the user to a lane or a scope with urgency and acknowledgement, impact analysis of a change on the lanes that are working, a staleness marker for what a lane was told, peer-to-peer sharing between lanes, or context for remote and cloud sessions that cannot read local files
data.falsifier: a command or event already addresses a message to a running lane, or tells which lanes a changed rule affects, or serves a pack to a cloud session
data.mechanism: event log with lamport marks and per-session cursors; doors a harness calls (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and tool hooks with additionalContext where they exist, MCP replies, heartbeat and wait elsewhere); handoff records (session.handoff) and fenced transfers (session.transferred); D-session-context bars ddflow from calling the remote-session tools of the host; harness-native message routes exist (Kilo prompt_async queues while busy, Claude SendMessage, Codex message to an agent thread, Cursor queued messages) and P-spawn.steer plans to use them for children only; remote and cloud agents see the repository and MCP/HTTP, not .ddflow/local
data.probe: inventory: B-rc-changes, B-rc-context, B-sc-transfer, B-sc-tree, B-sc-native-status, B-am-restart-brief, D-session-context, P-spawn, P-remote, P-multiuser; the agent reports for mid-session injection rungs
data.probe_output: B-rc-changes: one change feed, per-session cursor, delivered at doors, relevant_to filter, record kinds only; B-sc-transfer: addressed fenced hand-off pack, fork; B-sc-tree: parent/role/goal fields; no task addresses a free-text directive to a lane, computes which running lanes a rule or safeguard edit affects, marks a lane's context stale, records acknowledgement, shares notes between peers, or serves packs to remote sessions; others (general knowledge, not surveyed): Claude Code agent teams message teammates, Kilo/opencode prompt_async queues, Codex messages to agents, Cursor queued messages, VS Code handoffs, ACP prompt and cancel, the A2A protocol, blackboard and publish-subscribe designs
data.question: How does ddflow share context between sessions and agents, locally and remotely, and push a change from the master, a rule, a decision or the user into sessions that are already working?

data.body: Operator 2026-10-13: review how ddflow shares session context between sessions and between agents locally or remotely, and inserts context into working sessions on demand when the master session, a rule, the context or the user changes something. Research R-context-sync (CONFIRMED). Reuses, never duplicates: B-rc-changes and B-rc-context (change feed and relevance context at the doors), B-sc-transfer, B-sc-tree and B-sc-native-status (hand-off, tree, native status), P-spawn (steer, notify, lane notes), P-safeguards (delivery evidence, relevance), P-remote (event feed, serve), P-multiuser (clone sync), P-agent-parity (door rungs per harness). Every value is a knob (D-everything-configurable); small modules (D-small-files).
data.title: Live context: tell sessions, know who is affected, mark stale context, share between peers, reach remote sessions, with acknowledgement

data.body: A door table per harness as descriptor data ([doors]): session start, user prompt, pre and post tool (additionalContext or equivalent), compaction, subagent start and stop, notification, idle or stop, MCP reply, statusline, and the native routes (Kilo and opencode prompt_async with noReply or system, Claude SendMessage and hook additionalContext, Codex message to an agent, Cursor queued message). For each: can ddflow put text in, is it persisted in the transcript or only seen for that turn, size limit, and the rung it gives (native hook, plugin, MCP reply, poll). Probe where a harness is installed; absent = NOT VERIFIED. This decides how fast a pushed change can actually arrive.
data.title: Audit the injection doors per harness: what can reach a running session, when, and whether it stays in the model's context

data.body: ddflow tell <lane|session|item|phase|glob|all> --text ... | --ref <record id> [--urgency fyi|next-door|safe-point|now]: a message.sent event (fenced, redacted, bounded) addressed by identity or scope. fyi and next-door ride the change feed (B-rc-changes) at the next door; safe-point is delivered between gates; now uses the harness steer route (P-spawn.steer) and is refused where none exists, saying so. CLI and one MCP tool, one declaration. Who may tell whom: the operator anyone, a master its children and peers on its items, an agent only its master; rate limits and size caps are knobs. A message is DATA to the receiver, never an approval or a permission change (D-session-context).
data.title: ddflow tell: a directed message from the master or the user to a lane, a session or a scope, with urgency, delivered through the doors and recorded

data.body: Placeholder dependency replaced below. On any edit of a rule, safeguard, decision, lesson, the item a lane holds (body, globs, needs), a quota or governor pause, or a plan change, compute from the lanes ledger (B-gap-lanes) which live lanes it governs (their item globs, audience, scope, phase) and classify: BLOCKING (a new prohibition or a pause: delivered at the next door with urgency safe-point or now), CHANGES-YOUR-TASK (item or acceptance edit), FYI. The edit command previews 'affects 3 lanes: ...' and notifies by default for BLOCKING (knob). Batches within a window so ten edits are one notice.
data.title: Impact analysis: when a rule, safeguard, decision, lesson, item or plan changes, find the running lanes it affects and notify them by severity

data.body: Each delivery of a brief, claim guidance or dispatch brief records a context revision for the lane: a digest over the ids and digests of the governing records (item text, safeguards, rules, decisions, lessons, cards). ddflow lanes shows STALE when the current revision differs; at the next door the lane gets a DELTA (what changed, bounded), not the whole brief, and a full re-brief at a safe point when the delta is large (knob). A lane on a harness with no doors is marked UNREACHABLE-WITHOUT-POLL so the master knows.
data.title: Stale-context marker: what each lane was last told, a revision of what governs it, and a delta when it changes

data.body: A receiver acknowledges implicitly (it called a door after delivery) or explicitly (ddflow ack). message.seen events give latency from send to seen; a BLOCKING notice unseen after N minutes (knob) is escalated: to the master, then to the operator through the ask engine (P-remote.ask), and the lane is marked as possibly working on stale rules. Harnesses with no door get an instruction to call a cheap pull (the existing ddflow_brief or ddflow_lanes with a since cursor, no new MCP tool, tool budget) at every task step. Honest limit: ddflow cannot force a model to read.
data.title: Acknowledgement and escalation: seen events, unacknowledged BLOCKING notices escalate to the master or user, and door-less harnesses poll cheaply

data.body: ddflow share post|read|list --scope item|phase|glob|topic: append-only, fenced, size-capped, TTL, dedupe, subscribed by scope so a lane touching the importer sees what another lane found there, delivered at the doors as FYI. 1. DuckDB. Default: keep D-no-duckdb as is (SQLite FTS5 stays the only index, vectors for B-semantic-recall/B-ds-semantic in the same SQLite). Measured: FTS5 is 10-60x faster per query, 10x cheaper to start (19 ms vs 222 ms, 13.5 MB vs 66 MB RSS), has phrase/prefix/trigram DuckDB FTS lacks, updates incrementally; DuckDB FTS is a static snapshot installed from the network (not in the wheel), the file format needs EXPORT/IMPORT across versions, one writer process. 2. Rewrite. Default: no rewrite, no native module now. Thresholds proposed (stored as [perf] budgets, B-perf-bench): hook p50 over 300 ms idle after the Python fixes -> Rust/Go fast path for the hook subset only; fold+read over 3 s idle at the expected size after checkpoints -> PyO3 core; resident MCP RSS over 1 GB or an active log over 1M events -> same. Accept, change numbers, or drop.

4. Resident state. Default: the MCP server keeps the folded State cached by log digest (no new daemon; D-sched-no-daemon stands). Alternative: a long-lived command daemon for the CLI (rejected by default: a process to supervise per clone).
5. Order. Default: the cheap fixes ride in B-gap-log-scale (P-gaps core wave, already extended); the rest of this phase follows it.

Ask the operator, record the decision, write docs/ddflow/decisions/pipeline-requirements.md. One question at a time with the recommended default; record each answer verbatim (ddflow session prompt) and as a decision (ddflow decision add --globs ...). Do not start another B-pipe-* task first. Evidence: R-pipeline-configurable-today (CONFIRMED), R-pipeline-requirements-design (THEORETICAL), bug B-na-required-gate.

QUESTIONS AND RECOMMENDED DEFAULTS
1. Field or kind? DEFAULT: one optional `pipeline` field (a table) on the existing guidance record (rule or decision); no new kind, no new store, no new config file. Rejected: a pipeline-rule kind (a second engine beside the record surface), and growing [gates] with per-glob tables (invisible to search, brief and RAG, outside the waiver/deviation engine).
2. What may an effect say? DEFAULT: require=[gate...] (with optional after=), allow_na=[gate...] with a reason class, forbid_skip=[gate...], order=[[a,b]...], kinds=[...] (item kinds it covers), define={gate table} for a project-specific gate backed by a declared command (executable: approved by digest, inert until approved, B-gap-command-trust). Gate DEFINITIONS stay in [gate.*]; the record only names ids.
3. Strength. DEFAULT: reuse enforcement x override from B-goal-decide. MUST (block, waive|none): the gate cannot be dropped, skipped or made N/A; only a person's waiver (<=90 days, scoped to globs) lifts it. SHOULD (warn, deviate): the gate is added as recommended; an agent records an item-scoped deviation with a reason, answered before complete. MAY (advisory): listed in gate status, never refused. A deviation never lifts a MUST.
4. What does 'scope matches' read? DEFAULT: the existing Scope (globs, categories, gates) plus kinds and tags; globs are matched against the item's declared globs at claim and against the ACTUAL diff (changed_paths) at gate status and complete; a requirement that matches either one applies (additions can only grow); an allow_na needs the diff to MISS (declared globs alone never grant N/A: bug B-na-required-gate).
5. Resolution time. DEFAULT: at claim, recorded as a pipeline.resolved event (resolved gate list with the source of each, digest of rule and config inputs, engine version); re-resolved at gate status/complete: gates may be ADDED mid-flight (the agent is told which rule added it), never removed without a recorded N/A or waiver. A rule edit never silently changes an in-flight item.
6. Agent powers. DEFAULT: additive and free: add a gate to this item (reason required, event, shown in review and metrics, capped by [pipeline].max_added = 3 per item, then a note); N/A of a non-required gate not covered by a MUST: allowed with reason class and evidence; ANY weakening (remove a gate from a pipeline or kind, N/A or skip of a required/MUST gate, lower a reviewer/evidence requirement, edit [gates].required, demote a record's strength) becomes a pending proposal only a person clears (builds on B-org-agent-guard). Agent-authored requirement records start status proposed, additive effects only, active after the operator accepts (like decisions).
7. The four invariants. DEFAULT: shipped as an org-style floor that no project record can weaken: unavailable never passes (already structural), every pipeline gate carries an outcome (gates.require_outcome), a cross-family reviewer on authored tasks, a regression test for a bug. They become policy-tier knobs (B-org-agent-guard) and the resolver refuses a requirement whose effect would remove them.
8. Precedence. DEFAULT: the P-goals order (org floor > project MUST > accepted decision > principle > preference); additions COLLECT (union); removals use strictest-wins (any MUST require beats any allow_na); an order cycle is a doctor error and the base order stands. Not 'first match' (DMN first-hit hides rules).
9. Preview. DEFAULT: ddflow workflow preview (--kind, --globs, --tags) and workflow diff (this change vs current, over open items) on CLI and MCP; an enforcement tier 'evaluate' that resolves and reports but adds nothing (GitHub ruleset evaluate idea, Gatekeeper dryrun) for the first N days of a new requirement.
10. Versioning and skew. DEFAULT: unknown `pipeline` keys in a record are carried, not dropped; an engine that does not know the field refuses to complete an item that a block-level requirement covers (fail closed), warns for warn-level.
11. Sprawl brake. DEFAULT: [pipeline].max_added = 3, a requirement that adds a gate must name a gate with a command or an evidence contract (no pure-prose extra gates), requirements that fired on zero items in 60 days are listed for review (B-dec-review), and a rule count cap shared with [rules].

data.body:
Ask the operator, record the decision, write docs/ddflow/decisions/goals-principles.md. Ask them one at a time with the recommended default; record each answer verbatim (ddflow session prompt) and as a decision (ddflow decision add --globs ...). Do not start any other B-goal-* or B-prop-* task before this is answered.

QUESTIONS AND RECOMMENDED DEFAULTS (evidence: R-goals-existing-map, R-goals-principles-proposals-design):
1. Is a principle a new kind or a field? DEFAULT: a field, not a kind. Add one field to the guidance record, override = none | waive | deviate (how a finding is cleared), orthogonal to enforcement (how hard a finding is). Principle = enforcement warn + override deviate; rule = block + waive; org floor = block + none; preference = advisory. Vocabulary shown to people: MUST / SHOULD / MAY (RFC 2119) next to the enforcement word. Rejected: a separate principle store (a second engine to keep in step), and enforcement alone (a warn finding needs no answer, so a soft rule fails by silence).
2. Who may deviate from a principle, and does it expire? DEFAULT: the authoring agent records a deviation, item-scoped, reason required (evidence optional), no approval, no expiry (it dies with the item), always visible in brief, completion summary and the operator's decision list. Only block rules need a person's waiver (up to 90 days, approved by digest, unchanged). A deviation from a principle on a CHECK-LESS record (judged by a reviewer) is accepted the same way.
3. Must a principle finding be answered before complete? DEFAULT: yes for SHOULD with a mechanical check or a reviewer finding that cites the id; complete refuses (exit 3) listing the unanswered ones; an answer is comply (fixed) or deviate (reason). MAY findings never refuse. Gate OUTCOME stays passed (a principle is not a blocker); the ledger carries the answer.
4. Precedence order. DEFAULT: org floor > project rule (block) > accepted decision > principle > preference; nearest scope (gate, then globs, then category, then always) wins within a tier, then priority, then newest; unreconciled conflicts are a doctor note and a B-coh item, never a silent pick. Goals never override a rule or a principle. Extends D-rules-hierarchy (workflow enforcement > project rules > agent defaults); it does not replace it.
5. Goal record shape. DEFAULT: def-record kind goal; fields title, body, status (proposed | active | achieved | dropped), owner, target_date, parent (at most 2 levels), links (phases, tasks, decisions, research), key_results[] each {id, text, source = dag | metric | check | manual, ref, baseline, target, direction}. Progress is computed: dag = done share of the linked phases' tasks (tasks weighted equally; a removed or abandoned task leaves the count); metric = a named ddflow metric (B-gap-metrics); check = a command through the shared runner, operator-config or approved by digest only; manual = an operator attestation with a date that goes STALE after [goals].manual_stale_days (default 30) and is then reported unavailable, never green. Overall goal progress = the minimum-of-trajectory view is NOT used; show each KR and their mean, marked an estimate.
6. What does the brief show of goals? DEFAULT: at most 3 lines (active goals by priority: title, mean KR progress, weakest KR, days to target, stale flag), plus at claim the item's goal chain (task -> phase -> goal) labelled Direction, not a constraint; orphan work (completed items under no goal) counted in the roadmap and doctor, never a gate.
7. Proposal storage and triage states. DEFAULT: def-record kind proposal outside the queue (status proposed | adopted | deferred (snooze_until) | rejected | expired | superseded); adopt creates a task through services/items.add_task (dup check included) in a phase the operator names and links back; adopt/defer/reject are person-only (CLI; no MCP verb, like ddflow approve); reject REQUIRES a reason and is remembered: a new proposal whose fingerprint or similarity matches a rejected one is not filed unless it carries new evidence the operator can see. Rejected: proposal as a task state (every scheduler, board and next path would need to learn it), and proposal as a research record (no adopt/reject lifecycle).
8. Discovery cadence and budget. DEFAULT: OFF until the operator turns it on (job feature_discovery shipped disabled); then weekly by the calendar, or every 2 completed phases, whichever the operator picks; per run at most 3 new proposals; at most 7 open (proposed, undecided) at any time, and the job does not run while the cap is reached (backpressure); at most 20 000 reviewed tokens per run when B-gap-spend can measure it (UNAVAILABLE, not zero, when it cannot, and then the run cap is the turn cap); circuit breaker after 3 consecutive runs with zero adopted proposals (job pauses and says so in brief); stale undecided proposals expire after 60 days. The job files ONE research item (kind research) through the normal claim, so any lane may take it and quotas apply.
9. What may discovery read? DEFAULT: the repository, the ddflow log, its own research records, dependency advisories through the configured companions; the web ONLY if the operator enabled [discovery].web (default false); the log redaction profile is applied to every proposal body; no file contents above 40 lines are quoted. Org policy may force web off.
10. Scope. DEFAULT: goals and principles may come from an org bundle (P-org-config) as read-only team goals/principles; a project may add its own and cannot deviate from an org floor; proposals and deviations are always local to the project log; personal (local-only) goals are allowed under .ddflow/local and never reach the brief of other users.
11. Evaluation gate for turning discovery on by default. DEFAULT: never on by default; recommend turning on after B-goal-eval reports >= 3 runs with acceptance in 20-70 percent.

ACCEPTANCE: the answers are recorded as a decision with the reasons; the doc lists every question with the answer; the dependent tasks' bodies are amended if an answer differs from the default (ddflow update). Tests: none (docs only); gates: research, rules, docs.
SIZE: small. DOCS: docs/ddflow/decisions/goals-principles.md.

Record-surface contract extension 2026-10-11 (operator request, D-record-surface-contract, phase P-record-contract): three more questions, with defaults, so the goal, principle and proposal kinds meet the record contract. 12. Who may create, activate, edit, drop or delete goals and principles? DEFAULT: the CLI and MCP offer the same verbs to a person and to an agent; an agent's add or edit of a goal lands as status proposed, and a change that WEAKENS (a goal dropped or achieved, a principle demoted from MUST to SHOULD or MAY, a rule retired, enforcement lowered, override widened) is accepted but flagged 'changed by agent' in the brief, doctor and the change feed until the operator acknowledges it (`<kind> ack`, operator-only, B-rc-lifecycle); the operator can reverse it (restore). This is D-decision-management 2 applied to every guidance and goal kind. 13. Merge and split: may two goals, two principles or two open proposals be merged, and one split? DEFAULT: yes, through the record surface (B-rc-lifecycle): merge unions links, key results and tags and keeps both ids reachable (merged_from / successor); split creates parts with provenance.split_from and retires the original with split_into; a key result keeps its id when it moves so progress history survives; deleting is retiring (a tombstone with a reason), never a purge. 14. Defaults below are all 'off or advisory': an existing project changes nothing on upgrade.

QUESTIONS AND RECOMMENDED DEFAULTS
1. Document class. DEFAULT: a `contract` field on a document type (evergreen | point_in_time | generated) plus a `[docs.classes]` glob-to-contract map for documents with no type; an unclassified document is treated as point_in_time (the safe side) until the operator confirms; the confirmation is ONE group-level question (folder globs plus named exceptions), recorded as a doc.classified event with the operator's words, never decided by the agent per document. Shipped defaults: README/ARCHITECTURE/SECURITY/CONTRIBUTING evergreen; ADR, plans, specs, decisions, CHANGELOG, HISTORY, research point_in_time; region-owned exports generated. Existing [enforce].doc_exclude keeps working and is read as 'not checked'.
2. Where the review stamp lives. DEFAULT: the log (doc.reviewed event with sha, verifier, deferred count), never the file; an optional in-file stamp region is `[docs].stamp = off|region`, default off (a stamp in the file churns every clone and conflicts under P-multiuser).
3. Who may record a doc as reviewed. DEFAULT: `[docs].review_requires = cross_family` (the reviewer is not the editor and a different model family from the agent that edited), unavailable when no such reviewer ran (recorded unavailable, no review stamp); `any` and `off` selectable.
4. Auto-fix. DEFAULT: report only. `[docs.autofix].allow` is an empty list; the selectable classes are identifier, path, flag, config_default and (with the dictionary) deprecated_term; counts, bare line-number citations, absence claims, cross-reference targets, example structure, behavioural claims and claims whose ground truth is outside the repository are a FLOOR that can never be listed. Only evergreen documents; a missing counterpart is confirmed removed-versus-renamed from git history before it is called removed.
5. Terminology dictionary. DEFAULT: yes, as an opt-in definition-record kind `term` (term, definition, deprecated synonyms, scope globs, exceptions by path glob only, permanence temporary|permanent); empty on a new project; a check family `terminology` in `ddflow docs check`, warn by default, whole-word, evergreen documents only; code identifiers and UI strings are findings, never auto-fixed. Alternative: do not build it (use rules with forbidden_text).
6. Scenario cards. DEFAULT: a `scenario` document type (collection `docs/scenarios/{slug}.md`) with the sections Pre-state, Steps, Expected, Cleanup, Sharp edges and a required falsifier on every Expected line; a `scenario` gate that is NOT in the default pipeline (add it with `ddflow workflow pipeline`) and applies_when the item's globs touch the card's `covers` globs; a weekly sweep job shipped disabled. Results are scenario.ran events with one verdict per step (pass | fail | unavailable) and the observed value; unavailable is never pass. Alternative: keep scenarios as demos/ scripts only.
7. Review lenses. DEFAULT: the lens (a short intent line plus an optional prompt template) becomes data on the gate (`lens`, `lens_prompt`), replacing the two-entry constant _LENSES in ddflow/api/review.py; shipped lenses refute, intent (today's two), plus design, security and docs_claims; shipped gate `design_review` available but NOT in the default pipeline; the default pipeline is unchanged. Findings keep HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW.
8. Reviewer panel. DEFAULT: off. `[review.panel.<gate>]` members (reviewer names), min_members, verdict_rule (any_confirmed | majority | all), merge_floor (similarity for merging equal findings); every member must pass the independence rule; a panel with fewer than min_members available is partial/unavailable, never passed; the synthesis is the gate's record (one id for triage), each finding carries who found it and the agreement count.

10. Phase-level or task-level. DEFAULT: the claims review and the corpus checks run at the docs gate of a phase and in the docs-correctness schedule job; the scenario gate is task-level only when added.

Docs: docs/ddflow/decisions/pipeline-ideas.md.

The same paragraph then repeats "decided by operator" — so the second `decided by hy-commit-events` is a misattribution of an operator's decision to an automated agent. data.claim: Systems whose every proposal passes an automated verifier (FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, autoresearch) produce real results; LLM-judgement-only systems fabricate (AI Scientist v1: 42% of experiments crashed, 57% of manuscripts had wrong numbers). So ddflow should require a named verifier, a committed pre-registered plan, prediction-before-observation, a stop rule and budget, a mechanical citation and number audit, and a confidence ladder, expressed as DATA over engines it already has or has planned.
data.falsifier: If a seeded fixture with planted traps (a dead citation, a confirming-only test, a number not tied to a run, a forking path) passes the pipeline, or if a standalone research item cannot be completed without a code-style worktree, the design is wrong.
data.mechanism: A research workflow template (stages, verifier, stop rules, budget, roles, rules, output records) drives the existing per-kind gate pipeline (kind_pipelines.research) with command/agent gates; hypotheses, predictions, observations and ruled-out results are reasoning-log steps; evidence is claims with sources and grades; plans are a document type with a sha stamp; runs are job/scenario records; the skeptic is a cross-family review lens; re-verification is a watch; reuse is the record-contract context and RAG export.
data.question: How should ddflow run research of any kind (architecture, math, hardware, DSP, science, ML), standalone or as a phase of development, so it converges on a best answer and the result is recorded and reusable?

data.title: Research workflows: pre-registered plans, hypotheses and predictions, verifier-first runs, stop rules, audited evidence and shipped default workflows per domain, standalone or inside a development phase

data.body: Four template files plus fixtures, no code beyond the template engine. lit-review: decompose, parallel searchers, evidence table, contradiction pass, synthesis, citation audit; stop on saturation. hypothesis-test: at least three rival hypotheses incl. a null, discriminating tests ranked by diagnosticity, matrix, verdict. design-decision: criteria, options, time-boxed spikes, scored matrix, red team, output is a decision record linked to the evidence and rejected options. replicate: a different-family agent re-runs from the record alone and up- or downgrades confidence.
data.title: Shipped workflows, general: lit-review, hypothesis-test (ACH), design-decision (to a ddflow decision) and replicate

data.body: Verifier is the Lean compile, run as an allowlisted command gate; unavailable when absent. The reviewer checks the statement, not the proof (a compiling proof of a drifted statement is the failure mode). Stop: proved, counterexample, or N failed attempts recorded as open.
data.title: Shipped workflow conjecture-proof: formal statement, numeric and brute-force check, counterexample search, proof attempt, Lean check, statement-fidelity review

data.body: Verifier is the simulator (ngspice) against the spec plus a second-model cross-check of extracted values; operator-supplied bench measurements enter as run records. Stop: spec met with margin or the Pareto set stabilises.
data.title: Shipped workflow sim-trade-study: requirements, datasheet extraction with unit, condition and page cite, netlists, corner sweep, ranked BOM, bench check

data.body: Ground truth hidden from the estimator by the harness interface; headless script or notebook reproduces the numbers; metric table with error bars; stop on plateau over K variants.
data.title: Shipped workflow dsp-experiment: synthetic ground truth, estimator, metric sweep over SNR and seeds, baseline, real data last

data.body: Immutable evaluation harness, fixed budget, results table of every run kept or discarded; a gain counts only when reproduced on at least three seeds.
data.title: Shipped workflow ml-experiment: baseline, one change per run under a fixed budget, keep/discard, ablation, multi-seed confirmation, held-out set touched once

data.body: README section kept short with a link, per-workflow page generated from the template, help topic, driver text for agents, plain prompts.
data.title: Document research workflows: README section, help topic, per-workflow pages, driver and lane-brief text

data.body: Throwaway project; plan committed before runs; prediction before observation enforced; stop rule fires and is recorded; audit blocks a bad citation; skeptic is another family; result reused by a later item.
data.title: Acceptance: a standalone hypothesis-test and a phase-embedded design-decision run end to end from CLI, MCP and prompt on a fixture, and a replicate downgrades a planted wrong result

data.body: Ask (AskUserQuestion) with recommended defaults: (1) verifier required to start a research item, or advisory; rec: required, with an explicit 'none possible: judgement only' option that caps the confidence at asserted. (2) plan commit before execution: enforced block or warn; rec: block for the shipped workflows, warn for ad hoc. (3) confidence ladder asserted/supported/verified, with only verified citable as fact; rec: yes, mapped onto the claim evidence grade. (4) skeptic and replicator must be another model family; rec: yes (D-reviewer-trust). (5) which verifiers may run: allowlist by digest (lean, ngspice, pytest, notebook); rec: operator approves by digest, unavailable never passed. (6) shipped workflows set; rec: lit-review, hypothesis-test (ACH), design-decision, replicate first; conjecture-proof, sim-trade-study, dsp-experiment, ml-experiment second. data.question: How can ddflow write and maintain requirements (project, vendor, code), vendor-relationship documents and product-management documents as a reviewed pipeline, safely with untrusted vendor material?

data.body:
Operator 2026-10-13: investigate ddflow writing requirements (project, vendors, code) from research, and managing vendor-relationship and product-management documentation as part of the pipeline; what exists and is planned, what to reuse, agent cooperation, best practice and what other tools do, subagents, rules and policies.

Research note R-product-docs. Spec-driven tools (Spec Kit, Kiro, OpenSpec, BMAD, Tessl) are markdown and diffable but none shows independent-model spec review, regression-test rules, a lessons loop, or vendor and PM document types: that is the gap ddflow's gates fill.
Reuse (no second engine): structured items as definition-record kinds on the record contract (the pattern of goal, claim and proposal: B-goal-model, B-prop-model, P-record-contract); narrative documents as document types with generated regions (P-docs-generic, region engine); deterministic lint as data on the docs-check engine (B-dt-validate, P-pipeline-ideas terminology and claims review); traceability and suspect links on claims and anchors (B-rw-claims, TF-trace); sources checked mechanically (B-rw-sources); goals as the parents of requirements (P-goals); decisions as links (decision records); person-only adopt for agent proposals (B-prop-model, D-reviewer-trust); trust=external fencing and the capability envelope (P-safeguards); cadenced jobs for dates (P-schedule); operator questions as blocking items (B-am-operator-qa); version cut and completed tasks for release notes.
NEW code is only: the requirement and vendor record kinds with their lifecycle, the requirement lint rule set (EARS and smells) as data, hash-based suspect links and baselines, the quarantine store and the extract-with-quote step, computed scoring (RICE) and notice deadlines, and the shipped data (document types, roles, workflows).
Hard rules: a requirement has a source or stays proposed-by-agent; a person accepts it; the agent never sends, signs, accepts terms or commits spend and only drafts; vendor material is untrusted data, stored by reference and hash, never quoted into events, lessons or decisions when confidential; dates and scores are computed in code, not by the model. Everything configurable, small files, CLI+MCP+prompt, logged. Paced per D-usage-pacing-2026-10 unless the operator says otherwise.

Main findings in the report:
- **Verdicts:** TTCN-3 has five (`none`, `pass`, `inconc`, `fail`, `error`). Robot Framework has PASS, FAIL, SKIP and NOT RUN. The report recommends mapping `inconc`, `error`, skip and licence failures to ddflow's `unavailable`. It also recommends keeping the tool's own verdict alongside the mapped one.
- **Gherkin:** A corpus study found more than 4 in 5 steps are exact duplicates of another step. No agentic coding tool is known to check new steps against the existing step corpus. That supports adding a duplicate-step gate.
- **LLM-written RTL:** 44.2% of Verilog that passes benchmark testbenches still fails formal verification (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.08416). CVDP code generation tops out at 34% pass@1 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.14074). The report therefore proposes a layered oracle with a mutation check, and review by a different model family from the author.
- **LLM network configs:** GPT-4 drafts contain topology, syntax and semantic errors. A deterministic verifier giving localised feedback fixed them, so the report requires a verifier before review.
- **Result formats:** JUnit is the common denominator, since cocotb, Eclipse Titan and Cucumber can all emit it. Cucumber Messages (NDJSON) is the preferred Cucumber format, and Robot Framework uses `output.xml`.

data.body:
Operator 2026-10-13: research and plan sharing information, databases, lessons, session context, decisions, rules, goals, policies, subagents, companions and configurations across projects of a company or division through a remote knowledge database with a custom protocol (propose it), beyond the centralized policy already planned; reuse the core; everything in the config file, CLI, MCP and prompts.

Research note R-knowledge-hub (the research agent read the MCP, A2A, OCI, Electric, Nostr, Zep and Mem0 sources; several vendor features were snippets; Automerge, Matrix, Datomic and LangGraph store were not covered).
Proposal DKP (ddflow.kb/1): immutable content-addressed records, separate signed attestations (approval, scan, endorse, still-true, disputed), sequence-numbered NDJSON feed with opaque cursors and up_to_date/must_refetch lines, signed snapshots, search with a token budget and provenance, propose-only agent tokens with the trust label set by the server, tombstones with reason classes (leak purges), a scope tree as the only ACL unit, bi-temporal fields with review_by.
Layering and reuse: policy bundles (P-org-config: sources, layers, trust, lock, policy) stay the prescriptive channel and the only way to enforce; DKP is descriptive and advisory and lands in a separate local imported layer, never in project shards; precedence policy bundle > project operator records > org-endorsed > project-promoted > agent. The record contract (P-record-contract) gives history, change feed, RAG export and relevance context to every kind; the serve and auth work (P-remote) gives the hub's HTTP surface and tokens; trust fencing and the reviewer rule (D-reviewer-trust) give the injection defence; sessions and memory (P-agent-memory, P-context-sync) give the optional summary kind (default off); lessons promotion (P-lessons) and decision categories (P-decisions) give what is worth promoting; the extension seam (P-extension-seams) gives the transports as registry entries.
NEW: the envelope and verbs, the client (mirror, outbox, sync), the publish pipeline (scan, quarantine, promotion), the git-mirror transport, a reference hub, and the layer in the fold.
Rules: nothing from the hub ever carries a tool grant, hook or command (skills, subagents and companions arrive only through signed bundles); a failed sync is unavailable, never passed; the mirror serves stale reads with an as_of marker; secrets and personal data are scanned at publish; every setting is a knob in the file, CLI, MCP and prompts and every change is a logged event. So autonomy must be a per-class ladder (suggest, prepare, execute with approval, execute within budget) that only the operator raises, the oracle files and gate config must be outside the agent's write scope, every proposal needs evidence and a kill criterion, and the narrow execute-within-budget classes come last.

Research note R-autopilot (primary reads: Devin review, Darwin Gödel Machine, METR, Anthropic multi-agent, Böckeler; the rest snippets; OKRs, release trains, tech radar and debt registers not researched).
Design: autonomy ladder per proposal class L0 suggest, L1 prepare, L2 execute with approval, L3 execute within budget; default L0; only the operator raises a class; a failed canary, reverted merge or skipped gate demotes it; direction, new dependencies with licence or security impact, public API and architecture changes are capped at L2. Loop: observe, assess, propose, approve, execute, verify, learn. Proposal types: feature, refactor, debt, bug sweep, doc fix, dependency upgrade, architecture change, each with an oracle and a stop rule. Architect workflow (context, drivers as quality attribute scenarios ranked by the operator, options with spikes, evaluation with a different-family reviewer and a red team, decision as an ADR, fitness functions as gates, scheduled re-evaluation) and product-manager workflow (outcome, opportunity tree, assumption tests, RICE with confidence penalty, now/next/later view derived from the queue, delivery as stories, release metrics, outcome review).
Reuse (no second engine): proposals and person-only adoption and feature discovery (P-goals: B-prop-model, B-prop-discover), goals and progress (B-goal-model, B-goal-progress), typed observation proposals, retro, bounded experiments and effect measurement (P-observe), scheduled jobs and watches (P-schedule), decisions and ADR files and dependency policy (P-decisions), requirements, stories and product documents (P-product-docs), research workflows (P-research-flows), test workflows (P-test-flows), the governor and cost envelopes (P-governor, P-safeguards), spawn (P-spawn), lanes, metrics and spend (P-gaps), lessons promotion (P-lessons), the knowledge hub (P-knowledge-hub).
NEW: the autonomy class table and demotion logic, the protected-verifier rule, fitness-function records and gates, the architect and product workflows as template data, the calibration record, the kill switch, and the observation jobs not yet planned (debt and drift sweeps).
Rules: the agent never edits its oracle, the gate configuration, review prompts or cost limits; a proposal without evidence is rejected by the tool; ceremony scales with risk; open proposals per operator are capped; the discovery job that reads the web has no write access beyond its proposal and executors never read raw web content. Everything configurable, small files, CLI+MCP+prompt, logged. Filed per D-usage-pacing-2026-10.

chunk_findings.detail: The document records that "the operator MAY allow sending drafts through a configured channel (explicit opt-in per project)", i.e. it makes the no-send floor configurable downward. The stated task is to ask the questions with recommended defaults where item (5) is explicitly a non-negotiable floor: the agent "never sends, signs, accepts terms or spends, drafts only; rec: yes, not configurable below that". A decision record whose entire purpose is to be the source of truth for the policy (`ddflow decision show D-product-docs`) must not assert that the floor was lowered; an implementer reading `PD-no-send` will wire an outbound path that the task forbids, and the seeded evaluation ("must still catch an unsourced or injected case") has no case for outbound sending. If the operator genuinely overrode the floor, the override has to be recorded against the operator's own words, not as a derived "MAY" in the same paragraph as the accepted defaults.

chunk_findings.detail: The recorded decision turns the send prohibition into a configurable path: item (2) has the operator answering "Same, but the operator may allow sending drafts through a configured channel", the "Recorded reading" then makes a channel "configured by the operator per project", and the Consequences section rewrites PD-no-send to "no sign, accept or spend; send only through a channel the operator opted in per project, each message approved by the operator at send time". The task this document implements states the opposite and marks it as a floor: "(5) the agent never sends, signs, accepts terms or spends, drafts only; rec: yes, not configurable below that." A recommendation may be overridden by the operator, but this one is explicitly declared non-configurable, so a per-project opt-in channel is precisely the knob the intent forbids; the doc even tries to have it both ways by asserting "the agent only drafts" in the same paragraph in which it defines a channel the agent transmits through. Concrete failure: project P sets a send channel (the "explicit opt-in per project" the doc authorises); an operator approves a draft at send time; the agent transmits it — an outbound, vendor-visible message has been sent by the agent, which the stated floor says must never happen, and PD-no-send, renamed rather than kept absolute, no longer blocks it. If the operator truly chose that option, the conflict with the non-negotiable floor should have been surfaced as a blocked item (never filed as `accepted` with the constraint silently redefined), otherwise the option should not have been offered at all.

Look over Paseo.sh (https://paseo.sh/) and research how easy it will be to integrate ddflow to work with Paseo and be managed remotely with any of the supported Paseo agents. Check if there are features we need to develop, on top of what is already planned and if we have gaps to integrate to Paseo, please create a phase + tasks for us to implement that with the proper dependencies and preferably reusing existing code cores, functions or extensions. Do similar research for integration with the rest of the list bellow:

1. Paseo: The Comprehensive Daemon and Worktree Architecture
Paseo is recognized as one of the most robust, explicitly designed control planes for AI coding agents available on the market23. Unlike monolithic cloud platforms, Paseo operates on a composable, decentralized client-daemon architecture. A headless software daemon executes continuously on the remote machine, home lab, or cloud server, serving as the central orchestrator for any agent providers installed on that specific hardware23. Developers then connect to this remote daemon utilizing a variety of frontend clients, including a native desktop application, a web UI, or a fully native mobile application that offers complete feature parity rather than functioning as a rudimentary WebView23.
Paseo features built-in custom implementations for an extensive array of agents, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, OMP, Antigravity, and Muse Code, while maintaining broad, native support for any ACP-compliant agent engine23. A defining characteristic of Paseo's remote execution architecture is its meticulous approach to filesystem isolation via Git worktrees. When a remote agent session is initiated, Paseo automatically provisions a dedicated Git worktree, placing the agent onto an isolated branch23. This prevents simultaneous agents from colliding, overwriting files concurrently, or mutating the remote machine's primary working directory.
Furthermore, Paseo functions strictly as a control plane; it does not extract API tokens, bypass provider terms of service, or send proprietary code to external telemetry servers23. Remote access is facilitated through either direct local network connections, bespoke tunnels, or an optional end-to-end encrypted relay service, ensuring that enterprise codebases remain securely within defined perimeter boundaries23. The platform is highly extensible through a plugin architecture that allows developers to augment the UI with custom screens, alter agent lifecycles, and integrate novel MCP servers23.
2. AgentOS: The Terminal-Native Multiplexer for Web and Mobile
For software engineering teams seeking a lightweight, mobile-first web UI with deep roots in traditional Unix terminal management, AgentOS provides a compelling open-source, self-hosted alternative25. AgentOS natively wraps an array of AI CLI tools—including Claude Code, Codex, Aider, Gemini CLI, Pi, and the Kilo Code CLI—directly inside of tmux sessions25.
By executing every discrete agent session within an isolated tmux pane, AgentOS guarantees robust session persistence. If a developer closes their web browser on a desktop or loses cellular network connectivity on their mobile device, the agent continues operating autonomously in the background on the remote server25. The web-based interface acts as a multi-pane multiplexer, enabling developers to run up to four distinct agent sessions side-by-side25. Crucially, AgentOS can orchestrate tasks across multiple different machines simultaneously, provided they are accessible via SSH keys, allowing a developer to view local agent sessions side-by-side with remote cloud VM sessions in the same browser window25.
The platform leverages optimized Unix utilities, utilizing ripgrep for high-speed codebase searching and relying on shell scripts for automated environment setup25. Furthermore, AgentOS features a highly adaptable notification system, supporting integration with shell commands via AGENTOS_NOTIFY_CMD or direct integrations with external messengers like Telegram, alerting developers instantly when a remote agent completes a long-running refactoring task or encounters a blocking permission prompt25.
3. Harness Remote: The Session Continuity and Lineage Layer
Harness Remote approaches the problem of fragmentation by focusing specifically on cross-machine and cross-agent workflow continuity16. Positioned as a "local-first control plane for native AI coding-agent sessions," it does not attempt to replace the underlying agents by synthesizing a universal conversation model. Instead, the native sessions remain entirely authoritative; the specific coding agent retains total ownership over transcript semantics, reasoning logic, tool execution, and context memory16. Harness Remote serves purely as the supervisory layer over Codex, Claude Code, OpenCode, Oh My Pi, and Pi16.
The system organizes remote workloads into a strict organizational hierarchy: Machines, Projects, and Sessions16. The most unique architectural proposition of Harness Remote is its cross-agent continuation and handoff mechanism. A developer can initiate an exploratory task using OpenCode on a remote server, monitor its progress via an Android device using a secure QR-code-paired web interface, and subsequently hand off the session lineage to Claude Code if a stronger reasoning model is required to finalize the implementation16. This handoff transfers bounded, inspectable context (such as overarching objectives and decisions made) without losing the thread of execution. The architecture guarantees that source code and credentials never leave the remote machine, relying on trusted LANs or VPNs rather than exposing gateways to the public internet16.
4. Nimbalyst, Orca, and Emdash: Parallel Execution and Artifact Management
Additional platforms focus heavily on parallel execution paradigms and the integration of secondary design artifacts.
Nimbalyst provides an open-source visual workspace explicitly designed to run parallel agent sessions (supporting Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode) while centralizing project management26. Unlike tools focused purely on code generation, Nimbalyst provisions a Kanban board interface where markdown specifications, system architecture diagrams (via Excalidraw), data models, and mockups exist as first-class, editable artifacts26. Agents are capable of reading and updating these design artifacts concurrently with the codebase, mapping perfectly to workflows where agents are expected to maintain comprehensive documentation alongside their pull requests26.
Orca is engineered for extreme horizontal scalability, operating as a development environment for monitoring entire fleets of parallel agents26. It boasts native support for over 25 distinct built-in agent CLIs—including Grok, Claude Code, and OpenCode—alongside any custom CLI tool26. Orca supports a specialized headless VPS (Virtual Private Server) mode, enabling enterprise platform teams to launch, monitor, review, and merge code from dozens of independent agents operating simultaneously within isolated Git worktrees across a distributed network26.
Emdash provides a cleaner, localized, open-source approach to parallel agent execution26. While functioning primarily as a desktop application, it excels at auto-detecting installed provider CLIs (including Aider, Cursor's CLI, Qwen Code, Devin, and others)26. Emdash is tightly integrated with issue tracking systems, automatically pulling tasks from Jira, Linear, Asana, and GitHub26. For every assigned task, it provisions a discrete Git branch and worktree, empowering developers to dispatch multiple agents against the same objective and visually compare their competing code diffs before authorizing a final merge26.

It also has per-plane effort tables, kit lists, a list of 15 features ddflow still needs, a top 10 and a phased order.

Main conclusions:
- **Paseo is the best fit.** It has an SDK (`@getpaseo/client`) over WebSocket, a CLI, plugins, per-agent MCP injection, and a permission model. ddflow can run as an MCP server inside its agents, a lane backend over `paseo run --no-wait`, or a plugin. The plugin is the hard part.
- **Worktree ownership is the real conflict.** Paseo, AgentOS, Emdash, Nimbalyst and Orca each create their own worktrees. The docs don't say how any of them would adopt a worktree ddflow made, so ddflow needs `claim --adopt` (bind a claim to a worktree another tool created). That is feature #2 in the top 10.
- **An ACP wrapper is the highest-leverage new adapter.** A `ddflow acp --wrap <agent>` proxy would claim an item, set the working directory to the ddflow worktree and inject the ddflow MCP server. Paseo (custom `acp` provider) and Zed (`agent_servers`) both register agents this way, and Harness Remote uses ACP adapters. That adapters honor an injected MCP server and working directory is not verified.
- **Easy wins:**
  - AgentOS: calling `aos notify` as a notification sink, and adding ddflow to its MCP list.
  - Nimbalyst: a one-way mirror through the `nim tracker` CLI.
  - Harness Remote: rendering ddflow's session transfer packs into its handoff fields, which map almost one to one.
  - Claude Code Remote Control: ddflow can supply the `WorktreeCreate` hook so `--spawn worktree` uses ddflow-owned worktrees.
- **MCP tool-list size matters.** This session exposes about 170 ddflow tools, so a lean worker profile is needed before any of these planes load it.

- The Orca name also belongs to an unrelated Go project (`orca-cli/orca`). I covered `stablyai/orca`.
- Crystal, which I did not research.
- Conductor, whose docs page I read gave no API or config details.</result>

The intent states the question was asked with "lane backends allowed to start agents: operator-only templates (P-remote.launch rules); rec: yes" — i.e. the accepted answer restricts agent starts to operator-only templates and leaves lane backends operator-driven. Because the document itself declares that "the record in the event log is the source of truth" and it "Governs: … `integrations/**`", any downstream work (CP-backend-iface, CP-scoped-tokens) built from this text will implement a bot-start capability that the operator's accepted recommendation denied. data.decision: (1) Every tunable value is a knob settable by config file, CLI, MCP and a plain prompt (D-everything-configurable). (2) Every definition the roadmap adds is a record kind under the record contract RC1 to RC12 (D-record-surface-contract): workflow templates, gates, review lenses, roles, lint rule sets, importers, packs, jobs, safeguards, document types, fitness functions, kind descriptors and the new records (requirement, vendor, waiver, approval, attestation and the rest): add, edit, remove as a tombstone, merge, split, restore, review and history, search, recall, RAG export, and exposure to agents and sessions at start, claim and mid-session. (3) Every workflow ships as a default template and is overridable per project (and per org) through the layer stack; changing a default never overwrites a value someone set. (4) Every change and every use that matters is a logged event, enough to rebuild decisions and information by replay; a restore verb exists for every kind. (5) One shared core: before adding a function, search the code for an existing one (recall and the code index); a second implementation of the same behaviour is a defect found by the clone guard, the reuse review lens and the standards gate; new phases extend the shared engines (P-shared-engines) instead of building their own. (6) Files stay under 20 KB. Exemptions need a reason in the exemption lists, which only shrink.

Today nothing in the queue covers more than one project: only the org bundle fetcher, co-change checks, the multi-clone work and the hub and test-pin phases filed this session.
Design: a constellation manifest lists member projects (name, remote, role, trust); a spec is a record with owner, consumers, declared version, a model digest (canonical parsed form) next to the content digest, a named checker and compatibility level, a lifecycle and a source; references across projects are project:id@digest; breaking classification comes from a checker run, never an agent's opinion; consumers are edges with an impact query; a compatibility matrix of test results with SUT pins feeds a can-i-release gate; owners raise change requests with per-consumer state, waivers and a deprecation window; baselines freeze sets of spec versions and need a human approval (the ICD cut); a sibling project is mirrored read-only, trust=imported, and events reference sibling events by digest, never embed them; imported spec text is untrusted and scanned.

NEW: the manifest, the spec kind and six format-adapter groups, digest pinning across projects, consumer edges, the breaking-change gate, the matrix and gate, change requests, the sibling mirror, the library registry, the onboarding workflow and drift audit.
Rules: a non-owner never edits a spec, it becomes a change request; pins are by digest; sibling content is data, not instructions; a missing checker is unavailable, never passed; nothing here sends, signs or spends (D-product-docs-r3). Filed per D-usage-pacing-2026-10.

data.claim: Harnesses read each other's files (VS Code reads .claude/agents, Cursor reads .claude/skills, opencode falls back to CLAUDE.md, Claude reads AGENTS.md only when there is no CLAUDE.md), so duplicates are often double-loaded and dedupe needs a who-loads-what graph; conflict handling differs (Claude concatenates, VS Code has no defined order, Roo replaces a mode by slug), so contradictions must be flagged and never auto-resolved; formats churn (Codex prompts, Windsurf under Devin Desktop, Kilo config, Gemini CLI replaced in part by Antigravity), so adapters need version stamps; imports carry hidden-Unicode, secret and permission-widening hazards and size caps (Codex 32 KiB, Windsurf 12,000 characters). So: read-only scan and inventory first, AGENTS.md as the canonical always-on file with pointers instead of copies, digest manifests and managed markers with drift checks, backup and revert, plan/apply as a queue item, glob rules and skills before subagents and commands, and permissions, hooks and MCP secrets native-only until the operator accepts.
data.falsifier: If a seeded fixture with the same rule in five files, a contradiction, hidden Unicode, a secret and a permission-widening skill passes onboarding without a flag, or an apply cannot be reverted, or a native edit after emit is overwritten, the design fails.
data.mechanism: A data-driven adapter table per agent (glob, class, scope, loader semantics, also-reads, caps, version) drives scan, classify, dedupe and emit; canonical records are data-declared kinds with trust=imported; emit uses managed regions and a digest manifest (extending the install manifest of P-agent-lifecycle); drift and round-trip use a three-way compare against the last emitted content; everything is a plan applied through the normal queue with gates.
data.question: When ddflow is introduced into a project with an existing AI workflow (instructions, rules, skills, subagents, commands, hooks, MCP configs, permissions, memory and steering files), how can it import, dedupe, convert and then manage them for every supported coding agent so operation afterwards is smooth?
sources: https://docs.cursor.com/context/rules; per-agent paths for Cursor commands

data.body:
Operator 2026-10-13: when ddflow is onboarded on a project with a preexisting AI workflow, skills, agent specs and rules, how are they imported and managed from then on, for all supported coding agents, so the operation after onboarding is smooth; what exists, what to extend.

Research note R-ai-config-import (Claude, Codex, Gemini, Cursor, Copilot, VS Code, Windsurf, Cline/Roo/Kilo, opencode, Aider, Continue and others; paths for several agents are unverified and are probed first). Exists or planned today and extended, not duplicated: rules inventory and import (B-rules-inventory, B-rules-import), skills model, onboarding and sync (B-skills-*), subagent parse, onboarding and sync (B-sub-*), agent command adoption (B-adopt-agent-commands), instruction blocks and the region engine (B-tpl-*), the install manifest, verify, redo and offboard of P-agent-lifecycle, harness descriptors (P-harness-adapters, P-agent-parity.descriptor-v2), decision inference at onboarding (B-dec-infer). Gaps: ONE inventory and normalisation across all artifact classes, the who-loads-what graph, contradiction and duplicate detection, plan/apply/backup/revert, digest manifests with drift and round-trip, hazard scans, and the per-agent adapters.
Design: read-only scan then a human inventory; deterministic classification first, an LLM only to split monolithic files (a proposal, trust=agent); canonical records with extra.<harness> fields; AGENTS.md canonical and pointers instead of copies where the harness allows; copy-sync with managed markers and digests elsewhere; permissions, hooks, plugins, off-disk team rules and specs stay native-only records with a pointer and digest; the import is a plan applied as a queue item with its own worktree and gates, and is revertable; user edits outside managed regions are never touched.
Rules: nothing is overwritten without a backup; a contradiction blocks adopt until a decision; imported text is trust=imported data; a secret or hidden-Unicode hit blocks emit; user-scope files are hashed, never copied into the repo; everything configurable, small files, CLI+MCP+prompt, logged. Paced per D-usage-pacing-2026-10.
data.title: Import existing AI workflow: scan, inventory, dedupe and convert the instructions, rules, skills, subagents, commands, hooks, MCP and permissions a project already has, for every supported agent, then manage them from ddflow with drift detection and revert

data.body:

(3) contradictions and duplicates block adopt until a decision; rec: yes. (4) permissions, hooks, plugins and MCP secrets stay native-only until accepted; rec: yes. (5) emit by pointer first, managed-marker copy second, never wholesale rewrite of JSON or TOML; rec: yes. (6) user-scope files are hashed, never copied; rec: yes. (7) first agent groups: claude, codex, gemini family, cursor, copilot and vscode, opencode; others after; rec: yes. (8) absorb native edits back into canonical records on request; rec: yes. (9) a secret or hidden-Unicode hit blocks emit; rec: yes. Record D-ai-import and write docs/ddflow/decisions/ai-import.md.

data.context: Operator 2026-10-13 asked how a project's preexisting AI workflow (instructions, rules, skills, agents, commands, hooks, MCP, permissions) is imported and then managed for every supported agent; note R-ai-config-import.
data.decision: Operator 2026-10-13 (AskUserQuestion, OB-decide): (1) AGENTS.md is the canonical always-on file; pointers first (Claude gets a short CLAUDE.md that imports it), managed-marker copy with a digest second, never a wholesale rewrite of JSON or TOML. (2) The import is a plan applied as a queue item, reversible (backup, one commit, revert); contradictions block adopt until a decision, and a secret or hidden-Unicode hit blocks emit. (3) Permissions, hooks, plugins, MCP servers and the other formerly native-only classes are MANAGED LIKE THE REST (imported and emitted), not native-only; this differs from the recommendation. Recorded reading: the same plan, backup, revert, drift and secret and hidden-Unicode rules apply to them, and a plan that widens an agent's access (a permission, a skill's allowed tools, an MCP server) is flagged in the plan for review; MCP secrets stay references only. (4) ALL supported agents in one wave, not the recommended staged groups; unverified paths are still probed first and a path that stays unverified is not emitted. Remaining defaults as recommended: user-scope files hashed and never copied; absorb of native edits on request.

data.context: Operator 2026-10-13 asked how sister projects (microservices, submodules, monorepo or split repos) share requirements, specs, user stories, APIs, tests and integration documents and how an update propagates; notes R-constellation and the topology research.
data.decision: Operator 2026-10-13 (AskUserQuestion, CN-decide): (1) Transports: shared spec repo first, then a read-only git mirror of a sibling's event log, the hub later; spec identity is a model digest plus a content digest and pins are by digest; events reference sibling events by digest and never embed them. (2) Strictness: the breaking-change gate, the change-request merge gate, the non-owner-edit refusal and the can-i-release gate only WARN (findings shown at the gate, in review and in the brief); this differs from the recommendation, which was to block. The break class still comes from a checker, and a gate can be set to block per project or per spec lifecycle as a knob. (3) Topologies: the submodule umbrella is supported but optional (a child with its own .ddflow is a separate project with a submodule-of pointer, cross-boundary leases are refused, work is paired items); a monorepo is one log with a project attribute from projects.toml; propagation is pull-first through constellation sync with push optional; change requests are proven inside a monorepo first, then across repos. (4) Baselines: a spec baseline is APPROVED BY THE AGENT when its checks pass, with no human in the loop; this differs from the recommendation. Recorded reading: the approval policy is a per-baseline-kind setting; interface and spec baselines default to agent-approved on passing checks, while requirement baselines keep their own policy (D-product-docs-r3 person acceptance) because they share the engine but not the approval default; every approval is an event with the approving agent and its checks. Remaining defaults as recommended: adapters OpenAPI and protobuf first, then ASN.1, schema formats, YANG, DBC and register maps; imported requirement tools stay read-only with their source ids; deprecation window 90 days as a knob.

chunk_findings.detail: The recorded decision drops the "duplicates" half of the confirmable rule. The question put to the operator (intent item 3) was "contradictions **and duplicates** block adopt until a decision; rec: yes", and the operator accepted the recommended defaults except where the document explicitly flags a deviation (only items 3 — native-only classes — and 4 — one wave — are called out as differing). Line 11 in turn only says "contradictions block adopt until a decision, and a secret or hidden-Unicode hit blocks emit", and the **Consequences** and **Alternatives rejected** paragraphs never mention duplicates either ("Native-only for permissions and hooks; staged agent groups; scan-only; directly applied import with warnings only"). Given two identical entries in an existing setup — e.g. two `CLAUDE.md` rule blocks or two copies of the same MCP server definition — the plan produced under this record has no mandate to stop for a decision, so a duplicate is silently adopted and emitted, which is exactly the case the operator's accepted default was meant to gate. Either the deviation must be recorded as an explicit override, or line 11 must read "contradictions and duplicates block adopt until a decision".

Check this new kilo feature - will it be worth of use for ddflow? Can you research and decide? Make a research and make a proposal how ddflow could probe the stack and again using the agent + internet (assuming agent can search internet) to do a proposal, then the agent or operator to accept it? Codegude mcp could also provide rules and styles and tools for different stacks too. Check if such function could be useful as well when we do research workflow, or test workflow, or anything we have planned. See what we could extend from the current core functions and planned tasks if possible and add tasks and phases for the rest you decide

data.claim: Yes, as an opt-in, guarded capability. The Kilo MCP exposes two tools, search over an API catalog and call with error feedback naming missing fields, covering usage and spend by feature, day and month, agent profiles and variables (create, update, delete) and the cloud agent lifecycle (start, status, send, interrupt, delete), authenticated as the user. For ddflow that is (1) a lane backend for cloud agents, (2) a usage and spend meter source for the governor and spend ledger, (3) a profile store to sync with the canonical subagent and skill store, and (4) a design pattern: a large surface behind two tools, search and call, which is a way to keep ddflow's own MCP tool list small. Similar surfaces exist for Devin (mcp.devin.ai: sessions, playbooks, knowledge, schedules), GitHub (create_pull_request_with_copilot in the GitHub MCP server), Jules (REST alpha with requirePlanApproval), Codex (codex mcp-server with codex and codex-reply), Cursor (Cloud Agents API) and Claude Code (Remote Control). Risk: these act as the authenticated user and can delete agents and spend money, so they sit behind a tool allowlist and approvals, tokens never in the repo, and returned text is fenced data.
data.falsifier: If a fake platform server lets an agent delete a profile or start a billable cloud agent without an approval, leaks a token into the repo or the log, or obeys an instruction in returned text, the guard is wrong.
data.mechanism: A [platform] section in the harness descriptor (kind mcp, rest or cli; url; auth method; org header; capabilities; tool allowlist; verified flag), consumed by the lane-backend interface (CP-backend-iface), the meters (P-agent-parity.meters, spend ledger), the profile sync (B-sub-sync) and the MCP guard (B-sub-mcp-guard); ddflow's own search-and-call facade is measured by the MCP budget reporter.
data.question: Is the new Kilo MCP server (a hosted MCP for the Kilo platform API) worth supporting in ddflow, and do other agents have similar platform APIs or hosted MCP servers worth adding to the agent support?
sources: https://cursor.com/docs/background-agent/api/overview; seen as search snippets except the Kilo post

data.body:
Operator 2026-10-13: check the new Kilo MCP feature; decide if it is worth using in ddflow; if so add it to the agent support and check for similar features for the other agents.

Research note R-platform-mcp. Decision: yes, opt-in and guarded. Kilo's server (https://mcp.kiloapps.io/mcp, authenticate with kilo mcp auth kilo) gives two tools (search, call) over its API: usage and spend by feature, day and month; agent profiles and variables; cloud agent lifecycle. Similar surfaces were found for Devin, GitHub Copilot (through the GitHub MCP server), Jules (REST alpha), Codex (codex mcp-server), Cursor (Cloud Agents API) and Claude Code (Remote Control).
Reuse: harness descriptors (P-agent-parity.descriptor-v2), the lane-backend interface and control-plane work (P-control-planes), meters and the spend ledger (P-agent-parity.meters, B-gap-spend, P-governor), canonical subagent and skill sync (B-sub-sync, B-skills-sync), the MCP guard (B-sub-mcp-guard), the approvals engine and the MCP budget reporter (P-shared-engines), the fixtures and fake approach of the evaluation harness.
NEW: a [platform] descriptor section, per-platform adapters, usage-meter readers, profile sync, the guard rules for platform tools, and a ddflow search-and-call facade.
Rules: opt-in per project (an adopt entry is written disabled until the operator enables it); tokens never stored in the repo or log, authentication stays with the agent's own flow; the platform acts as the user, so deletes, spend and cross-org actions need an approval and the org is always explicit; returned text is fenced data; everything configurable, CLI+MCP+prompt, logged. Paced per D-usage-pacing-2026-10.

**Recommendation:** Yes, ddflow should probe the stack and propose per-stack tools as companions. It should do this from a data-driven catalogue first, then an optional agent+internet step for tools the catalogue lacks. Those agent-proposed additions would carry trust=agent, `verified: false`, and need the operator's explicit accept.

**Caveats:**
- **Fetch quality:** WebFetch returns a small-model summary, so [FETCHED] means "fetched", not "quoted exactly".
- **Unchecked rows:** Most per-tool rows in the stack-by-stack landscape (item 2) are [UNVERIFIED] because I did not fetch them. That covers Go, Java, C/C++ and Solidity tools, for example. The report says each row needs checking before it goes into the catalogue.
- **Weak sources:** The reward-hacking and Serena token-saving claims come from blogs and search snippets, not primary studies.

**Creusot:**
- **What it is:** A deductive verifier for Rust at version 0.14.0, so pre-1.0. It translates Rust to Coma, then uses Why3 and SMT solvers (z3, cvc5, alt-ergo). It is LGPL-2.1.
- **Install:** Needs `opam`, and `./INSTALL` takes several minutes. The commands to run it and its output format were not confirmed.
- **Where it fits:** As an opt-in verifier named in the research/test workflows, never a default gate. Kani is the better first Rust verifier: `cargo install --locked kani-verifier`.
- **LLM evidence:** I found no Creusot-specific LLM paper. The nearest evidence is AutoVerus (>90% of 150 Verus proof tasks solved) and VeruSAGE-Bench.
- **Main risk:** The agent weakens the spec, or adds trusted/assumed escapes, to turn the prover green. The proposed fix is to count trusted/assumed items against main.

**Proposal highlights:**
- **Probe:** `ddflow companions probe` is deterministic and needs no network. It scans manifests, existing tool configs, CI commands and language mix, and does not install anything.
- **Records:** Accept and decline are events. Declined means the gate records `unavailable`.
- **Gate rules:** New suppressions (`eslint-disable`, `assume`, trusted markers) are counted and shown to review. Agents may not edit tool configs or test files alongside the code they check without the reviewer seeing it. Dismissed findings need a recorded reason.
- **Install safety:** ddflow prints the exact install command and never runs it. It prefers pinned, checksummed paths over `curl | bash`. Newly installed MCP servers get their tool descriptions hashed at accept-time.

**Top 10, in order:**
1. Linters already configured in the repo.
2. Dependency and licence checks, such as cargo-deny.
3. Type checkers.
4. Faster test runners (nextest, pytest-xdist), which also address the known `unit_tests` gate timeout.
5. LSP MCP servers (mcp-language-server, Serena), advisory only.
6. Shell, Docker and IaC linters.
7. Kani or CBMC.
8. Property-based testing.
9. Mutation testing on changed code.
10. Opengrep and ast-grep for project-specific rules.

Creusot, Verus, Dafny, GNATprove and the other proof tools are deferred as opt-in. Licences to note: Serena's core is GPL-3.0, so run it as a separate process and do not bundle it. Creusot and Opengrep are LGPL-2.1.</result>

data.claim: Yes: a deterministic probe (manifests, existing tool configs, CI commands, language mix; no network, no install) feeding a data-driven catalogue of tools per stack and role, an optional agent-plus-internet step for tools beyond the catalogue (trust=agent, verified false, cited, operator accepts), and accept or decline recorded as events (declined means the gate records unavailable). Order of value: linters already configured in the repo, dependency and licence checks, type checkers, faster test runners, LSP MCP servers (advisory), shell/Docker/IaC linters, then Kani or CBMC, property-based tests, mutation on changed code, ast-grep or Opengrep rules; deductive provers (Creusot 0.14, pre-1.0, needs opam; Verus, Dafny, SPARK) are opt-in verifiers named by a workflow, not default gates. Main risks: the agent weakens specs or adds trusted/assume/suppression escapes to turn a tool green, installs are supply-chain events, tool descriptions of new MCP servers can poison, and licences (Serena GPL-3.0 core: run as a separate process).
data.falsifier: If a fixture lets an agent pass a gate by adding a suppression, weakening a tool config or marking a proof trusted without review noticing, installs a tool without an accepted proposal, or accepts a poisoned MCP tool description, the guards are wrong.

<note>A task-notification fires each time this agent stops with no live background children of its own. The user can send it another message and resume it, so the same task-id may notify more than once.</note>
<result>I wrote the report to `/tmp/claude-1001/-home-delian-src-ddflow--claude-worktrees-bridge-cse-016cBDq3Gc6ZdGcaDbgG4Fz9/51a68c9d-2f99-5e8c-a18a-f9c8ae5cc561/scratchpad/acp.md`. It is about 3,500 words, a bit over the 3,000 target. Every claim carries a source URL and a [FETCHED-RAW], [FETCHED], [SNIPPET], [INFERRED] or [UNVERIFIED] tag.

**Recommendation**
- **ddflow as ACP client (do this):** it gives one lifecycle (start, stream, cancel, resume) across about 20 agents. `session/new` carries `cwd` and `mcpServers`, so the ddflow MCP server is injected natively.
- **`ddflow acp --wrap` (do it second):** it mainly rewrites `session/new`, so it comes after the client exists. The formal route is the proxy-chains RFD (`proxy/successor` plus a "conductor"), which is still a draft with only prototype Rust crates, so I'd keep a private wrapper for now.
- **ddflow as ACP agent (no):** editors want a model-driven agent, and ddflow is a queue.
- **Remote transport (don't build on it yet):** the HTTP and WebSocket transport is only an RFD. Today's options are Copilot's TCP mode, Droid's `acp-daemon`, or stdio over ssh.

**Protocol state**
- **v1:** stable. The latest schema tag is `schema-v1.25.0` (2026-10-09), so it keeps getting additive features.
- **v2:** draft. It removes the `fs/*` and `terminal/*` client methods and `session/load`. `session/prompt` also returns on message insertion rather than turn end. So I'd advertise no fs/terminal capabilities and isolate the turn-completion logic.
- **SDKs:** official ones exist for TypeScript, Python, Rust, Kotlin and Java. The Python one is the likely fit; I assume ddflow is Python from the uv/pytest notes.
- **Registry:** the live file lists 41 agents, so launch commands can come from it instead of being hardcoded.
- **Conformance:** `acp-tck` is experimental and tests agents, not clients. Its `conforming.py` fixture is a starting point for the fake agent.

**What ACP cannot do for ddflow**
- **Hooks:** ACP has no hook concept, so gate enforcement stays in per-agent hooks and MCP. The Stop-hook substitute is a controller loop that re-prompts after `end_turn`.
- **Claude adapter and hooks [INFERRED]:** the adapter loads user, project and local settings, so hooks should still fire. I did not run it to confirm that, or that a Stop-hook block continues the turn. Task 1 in the report is a spike to settle this.
- **Steering:** it is not in the standard. The Claude adapter uses a custom `_session/steering` method, and Codex's own app-server has native `turn/steer`.
- **Agent fidelity:** native APIs beat ACP for claude, codex and opencode. The report suggests ACP as a generic backend alongside native ones.

**Adapter table (section 5, from the registry JSON)**
- **Native:** gemini, copilot (public preview), kilo, cursor, kimi, opencode, qwen, devin, cline, goose, junie, augment and grok. Droid has an ACP mode, and antigravity ships a Google ACP server binary.
- **Adapter:** claude and codex use the official adapters. amp, pi and glm use community or third-party ones.
- **Native, not in the registry:** openhands (`openhands acp`, from its docs; its permissions support looked incomplete).
- **No ACP agent (client-side only):** vscode, zed and windsurf.
- **Nothing found:** qodo, tabnine, aider, replit, cody, roo and continue. I could not verify these. They stay on tmux.

**Not verified**
- **Harness Remote:** I could not find it at all.
- **Paseo:** its README never mentions ACP. The ACP-provider claim comes only from a search snippet, because the DeepWiki page returned 429.
- **Fetch quality:** many WebFetch results were summarized by a small model, so those details are probable rather than verbatim. The raw downloads (registry, schema meta, adapter source, TCK) are solid.
- **Python SDK client side:** I did not read its client API.
- **Per-agent cancel behaviour:** I did not test it.

The report also covers the comparisons with MCP, A2A, the opencode server, the Claude SDK and the Codex app-server. It ends with pros and cons, gaps and risks, 10 tasks, the fake agent and fake client test designs, and the ranked top 10.</result>
